lessons.title: 8.1 Perimeter and Area
lessons.notes_html:
Introduction

In our daily routine we observe many objects, figures and shapes which look like geometrical shapes, such as square, rectangle and triangle, etc. These are 2-Dimensional figures.

Similarly, we also observe and use different types of solid objects, such as ball, table, milk box, match box and fridge etc. These are all 3-dimensional objects, e.g. look at the matchbox, it has 6-faces, 8-vertices and 12-edges.

Perimeter

“The distance around any 2-dimensional closed shape is called perimeter.”

  • The length of fence around the field.
  • The length of floor of your room.
  • The total length of all sides of front page of your math book.

Mostly the distance and length is measured in kilometre (km), metre (m) and millimetre (mm).

Area

The region enclosed within a boundary of a closed shape is called area.

  • The cost of weeding in the plot.
  • The number of tiles in the wall.
  • The cost of painting the wall.

mcqs.q: What is the perimeter of a 2-dimensional closed shape?
options: The region enclosed inside the shape
The number of faces of the shape
The space occupied by a solid object
mcqs.why: The notes define perimeter as the distance around any 2-dimensional closed shape, measured along its boundary.

mcqs.q: Which group contains only 2-dimensional figures named in the lesson?
options: Milk box, match box and ball
mcqs.why: Square, rectangle and triangle are given in the lesson as examples of 2-dimensional geometrical figures seen in daily life.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a 3-dimensional object named in the lesson?
mcqs.why: The match box is listed with ball, table, milk box and fridge as a 3-dimensional solid object, unlike the flat 2-dimensional shapes.

mcqs.q: How many faces does a matchbox have, as stated in the lesson?
mcqs.why: The lesson describes the matchbox as a 3-dimensional object having 6 faces, 8 vertices and 12 edges, so it has 6 faces.

mcqs.q: How many vertices does a matchbox have, as stated in the lesson?
mcqs.why: The lesson states that a matchbox has 6 faces, 8 vertices and 12 edges, so the number of vertices is 8.

mcqs.q: How many edges does a matchbox have, as stated in the lesson?
mcqs.why: The lesson states that a matchbox has 6 faces, 8 vertices and 12 edges, so the number of edges is 12.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an example of perimeter given in the lesson?
options: The length of fence around a field
The cost of painting a wall
The number of tiles in a wall
The cost of weeding in a plot
mcqs.why: A fence runs around the boundary of the field, so its length is the distance around the field, which is a perimeter example.

mcqs.q: What is the area of a closed shape?
options: The total length of all its sides
The height of the shape above sea level
The region enclosed within the boundary of the shape
mcqs.why: The notes define area as the region enclosed within a boundary of a closed shape, not the distance around it.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an example connected with area in the lesson?
options: The length of fence around a field
The total length of all sides of the front page of a maths book
The cost of painting a wall
The length of the floor of a room
mcqs.why: Paint covers the region enclosed by the wall's boundary, so the cost of painting a wall is given as an area example.

mcqs.q: In which units are distance and length mostly measured, according to the lesson?
mcqs.why: The lesson states that mostly the distance and length is measured in kilometre (km), metre (m) and millimetre (mm).

lessons.title: 8.1.1 Recognization of Formulae to Calculate the Area and Perimeter
lessons.notes_html:
Formulae for area and perimeter of square and rectangle

The following are some important results we covered in our primary classes to calculate the perimeter and area of square and rectangle (ℓ = length/side, b = breadth):

NamePerimeterArea
SquareP = Sum of all sides = ℓ + ℓ + ℓ + ℓ = 4ℓA = ℓ × ℓ = ℓ²
RectangleP = Sum of all sides = ℓ + b + ℓ + b = 2ℓ + 2b = 2(ℓ + b)A = ℓ × b

Perimeter of square: P = 4ℓ

Area of square: A = ℓ²

Perimeter of rectangle: P = 2(ℓ + b)

Area of rectangle: A = ℓ × b

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the perimeter of a square, where ℓ is the side?
mcqs.why: Perimeter of a square = sum of all sides = ℓ + ℓ + ℓ + ℓ = 4ℓ, as given in the formulae table of this lesson.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the area of a square, where ℓ is the side?
mcqs.why: Area of a square = ℓ × ℓ = ℓ², as given in the formulae table; 4ℓ is its perimeter, not its area.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the perimeter of a rectangle, where ℓ is length and b is breadth?
mcqs.why: Perimeter of a rectangle = ℓ + b + ℓ + b = 2ℓ + 2b = 2(ℓ + b), as given in the formulae table of this lesson.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the area of a rectangle, where ℓ is length and b is breadth?
mcqs.why: Area of a rectangle = length × breadth = ℓ × b, as given in the formulae table; the other expressions belong to perimeters.

mcqs.q: In these formulae, what does the symbol ℓ stand for?
mcqs.why: The lesson introduces the formulae with ℓ = length/side and b = breadth, so ℓ stands for the length or the side.

mcqs.q: In these formulae, what does the symbol b stand for?
mcqs.why: The lesson introduces the formulae with ℓ = length/side and b = breadth, so the symbol b stands for breadth.

mcqs.q: How is the perimeter of a square written as a sum of its sides?
mcqs.why: A square has four equal sides, so its perimeter = sum of all sides = ℓ + ℓ + ℓ + ℓ, which simplifies to 4ℓ.

mcqs.q: How is the perimeter of a rectangle written as a sum of its sides?
mcqs.why: A rectangle's sides are length, breadth, length, breadth, so its perimeter = ℓ + b + ℓ + b = 2(ℓ + b).

mcqs.q: Which expression is equal to 2(ℓ + b) for the perimeter of a rectangle?
mcqs.why: The table shows the rectangle's perimeter as ℓ + b + ℓ + b = 2ℓ + 2b = 2(ℓ + b), so 2ℓ + 2b is the equal expression.

mcqs.q: How is the area of a square written as a multiplication?
mcqs.why: The table gives the area of a square as A = ℓ × ℓ = ℓ², multiplying the side by itself; ℓ × b is a rectangle's area.

lessons.title: 8.1.2 Calculation for Perimeter and Area of a Square and Rectangle
lessons.notes_html:
Perimeter and area of square

Perimeter and area of square and rectangle can be found by using the formulae given in section 8.1.1.

Example 1 — Find the perimeter of square whose length of each side is 5 cm

Step 1: Length of each side of square = ℓ = 5 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Perimeter of square = P = 4ℓ

Step 3: Substitute ℓ = 5: P = 4 × 5 = 20 cm.

Final answer: The perimeter of the square is 20 cm.

Example 2 — Find the area of square if the length of each side of square is 6 cm

Step 1: The length of each side of square = 6 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of square = A = ℓ²

Step 3: Substitute ℓ = 6: A = (6)² = 6 × 6 = 36 cm².

Final answer: The area of the square is 36 cm².

Example 3 — The length of each side of square flower bed is 8 m. The cost of flowering is Rs. 30 per square metre and the cost of fencing is Rs. 20 per metre. Find the total cost of flowering and fencing the flower bed.

Step 1: Length of each side of flower bed = ℓ = 8 m. Cost of flowering = Rs. 30 per square metre. Cost of fencing = Rs. 20 per metre.

Step 2: Write the formula: Perimeter of square = P = 4ℓ

Step 3: Perimeter of flower bed = 4(8) = 32 m. So the total length of fence is 32 m.

Step 4: Cost of fencing = 20 × 32 = Rs. 640.

Step 5: Write the formula: Area of square = A = ℓ²

Step 6: A = (8)² = 8 × 8 = 64 m².

Step 7: Total cost of flowering = 30 × 64 = Rs. 1920.

Final answer: The total cost of flowering is Rs. 1920 and the total cost of fencing is Rs. 640.

Perimeter and area of rectangle

Example 4 — Find the perimeter of the rectangle having length of 6 cm and breadth of 4 cm

Step 1: Length of rectangle = ℓ = 6 cm, breadth of rectangle = b = 4 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Perimeter of rectangle = P = 2(ℓ + b)

Step 3: Substitute: P = 2(6 + 4) = 2(10) = 20 cm.

Final answer: The perimeter of the rectangle is 20 cm.

Example 5 — Find the area of the rectangle having length of 5 cm and breadth of 4 cm

Step 1: Length of rectangle = ℓ = 5 cm, breadth of rectangle = 4 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of rectangle = A = Length × Breadth = ℓ × b

Step 3: Substitute: A = 5 × 4 = 20 cm².

Final answer: The area of the rectangle is 20 cm².

Example 6 — Neelam made a Pakistani national flag for the national day. The flag is 2 m wide and 3 m long. The cost of cloth used in flag is Rs. 75 per m² and that of the lace used around the flag is Rs. 10 per metre. How much money did she spend to make the flag?

Step 1: The length of flag = ℓ = 3 m, breadth of flag = b = 2 m.

Step 2: Write the formula: Perimeter of rectangle = P = 2(ℓ + b)

Step 3: Perimeter of flag = 2(3 + 2) = 2(5) = 10 m. So Neelam used 10 m of lace around the flag.

Step 4: Cost of lace for 1 metre = Rs. 10, so cost of lace for 10 metre = 10 × 10 = Rs. 100.

Step 5: Write the formula: Area of rectangle = A = ℓ × b

Step 6: Area of flag = 3 × 2 = 6 m². So Neelam used 6 m² of cloth to make the flag.

Step 7: Cost of cloth for 1 m² = Rs. 75, so cost of cloth for 6 m² = 75 × 6 = Rs. 450.

Step 8: Total cost of the flag = 100 + 450 = Rs. 550.

Final answer: Neelam spent Rs. 550 to make the flag.

Example 7 — Find the breadth of a rectangular field with length 20 m and area 315 m². Also find the perimeter of the rectangular field.

Step 1: Area of rectangular field = 315 m², length of rectangular field = 20 m.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of rectangle = length × breadth, so Breadth = Area of rectangle / Length.

Step 3: Breadth = 315/20 = 15.75 m.

Step 4: Write the formula: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(length + breadth) = 2(ℓ + b)

Step 5: Perimeter = 2(20 + 15.75) = 2(35.75) = 71.50 m.

Final answer: The breadth of the rectangular field is 15.75 m and its perimeter is 71.50 m.

Worked examples — Practice-1 (find the area and perimeter of the rectangles)

(i) length = 7 cm, breadth = 5 cm

Step 1: Write the formulae: Area of rectangle = ℓ × b and Perimeter of rectangle = 2(ℓ + b).

Step 2: Area = 7 × 5 = 35 cm².

Step 3: Perimeter = 2(7 + 5) = 2(12) = 24 cm.

Final answer: Area = 35 cm², Perimeter = 24 cm

(ii) length = 15 cm, breadth = 13 m (units as printed in the book)

Step 1: Write the formulae: Area of rectangle = ℓ × b and Perimeter of rectangle = 2(ℓ + b).

Step 2: Area = 15 × 13 = 195 square units.

Step 3: Perimeter = 2(15 + 13) = 2(28) = 56 units.

Final answer: Area = 195 square units, Perimeter = 56 units

mcqs.q: Find the perimeter of a square whose length of each side is 5 cm.
mcqs.why: Perimeter of a square: P = 4ℓ. Working: P = 4 × 5 = 20 cm, which is Example 1 of this lesson.

mcqs.q: Find the area of a square if the length of each side is 6 cm.
mcqs.why: Area of a square: A = ℓ². Working: A = (6)² = 6 × 6 = 36 cm², which is Example 2 of this lesson.

mcqs.q: A square flower bed has side 8 m. Fencing costs Rs. 20 per metre. What is the total cost of fencing the flower bed?
mcqs.why: Perimeter of a square: P = 4ℓ = 4 × 8 = 32 m of fence. Cost of fencing = 20 × 32 = Rs. 640, from Example 3.

mcqs.q: A square flower bed has side 8 m. Flowering costs Rs. 30 per square metre. What is the total cost of flowering the flower bed?
mcqs.why: Area of a square: A = ℓ² = (8)² = 64 m². Cost of flowering = 30 × 64 = Rs. 1920, from Example 3 of this lesson.

mcqs.q: Find the perimeter of a rectangle having length 6 cm and breadth 4 cm.
mcqs.why: Perimeter of a rectangle: P = 2(ℓ + b). Working: P = 2(6 + 4) = 2(10) = 20 cm, which is Example 4.

mcqs.q: Find the area of a rectangle having length 5 cm and breadth 4 cm.
mcqs.why: Area of a rectangle: A = ℓ × b. Working: A = 5 × 4 = 20 cm², which is Example 5 of this lesson.

mcqs.q: Neelam's flag is 3 m long and 2 m wide. Cloth costs Rs. 75 per m² and lace around the flag costs Rs. 10 per metre. How much did she spend in total?
mcqs.why: Perimeter: P = 2(ℓ + b) = 2(3 + 2) = 10 m, so lace costs 10 × 10 = Rs. 100. Area: A = ℓ × b = 3 × 2 = 6 m², so cloth costs 75 × 6 = Rs. 450. Total = 100 + 450 = Rs. 550.

mcqs.q: A rectangular field has length 20 m and area 315 m². Find its breadth.
mcqs.why: Area of a rectangle: A = length × breadth, so breadth = Area / length. Working: breadth = 315 / 20 = 15.75 m, from Example 7.

mcqs.q: A rectangular field has length 20 m, area 315 m² and breadth 15.75 m. Find its perimeter.
mcqs.why: Perimeter of a rectangle: P = 2(ℓ + b). Working: P = 2(20 + 15.75) = 2(35.75) = 71.50 m, from Example 7.

mcqs.q: Find the area and perimeter of a rectangle with length 7 cm and breadth 5 cm.
mcqs.why: Area of a rectangle: A = ℓ × b = 7 × 5 = 35 cm². Perimeter of a rectangle: P = 2(ℓ + b) = 2(7 + 5) = 2(12) = 24 cm.

lessons.title: 8.1.3 Find Area of Path (Inside or Outside) of a Rectangle or Square
lessons.notes_html:
Area of path (inside or outside)

We have learnt about perimeter and area of square and rectangle. Now we will discuss about the area of path (inside or outside). It is observed that in a rectangular or square park, garden, field, etc., some space in the form of paths is left inside or outside. We will use the concept of the area of square and rectangle to determine the area of different paths.

In the book's figure of a rectangle, the coloured portion represents the area of path:

Area of large rectangle = Outer length × Outer breadth

Area of small rectangle = Inner length × Inner breadth

Area of path = Area of large rectangle − Area of small rectangle = (outer length × outer breadth) − (inner length × inner breadth)

Remember: If the path lies all around the park on the outside, then the length of the park including the path = length of the park + 2 × width of the path. Similarly, the breadth of the park including the path = breadth of the park + 2 × width of the path.

Example 8 — A rectangular park of length 80 m and breadth 50 m is to be surrounded externally by a path which is 4 m wide. Find the cost of turfing the path at the rate of Rs. 200 per m². (Solved as in the book, taking 80 m × 50 m as the outer measurement including the path.)

Step 1: Length of park with path = 80 m, breadth of park with path = 50 m.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of rectangle = length × breadth. Area of park with path = A₁ = outer length × outer breadth = 80 × 50 = 4000 m².

Step 3: Inner length = 80 − (2 × 4) = 80 − 8 = 72 m. Inner breadth = 50 − (2 × 4) = 50 − 8 = 42 m.

Step 4: Area of park without path = A₂ = inner length × inner breadth = 72 × 42 = 3024 m².

Step 5: Write the formula: Area of path = A₁ − A₂. Area of path = 4000 − 3024 = 976 m².

Step 6: Cost of turfing on 1 m² = Rs. 200, so cost of turfing on 976 m² = 200 × 976 = Rs. 195,200.

Final answer: The cost of turfing the park path is Rs. 195,200.

Worked examples — Exercise 8.1, Question 1: Find the perimeter of the following shapes

(i) Square of side 3.7 cm

Step 1: Write the formula: Perimeter of square = P = 4ℓ

Step 2: P = 4 × 3.7 = 14.8 cm.

Final answer: 14.8 cm

(ii) Rectangle of length 4.5 cm and breadth 2 cm

Step 1: Write the formula: Perimeter of rectangle = P = 2(ℓ + b)

Step 2: P = 2(4.5 + 2) = 2(6.5) = 13 cm.

Final answer: 13 cm

(iii) Square (shown as a diamond) of side 4 cm

Step 1: Write the formula: Perimeter of square = P = 4ℓ

Step 2: P = 4 × 4 = 16 cm.

Final answer: 16 cm

(iv) Rectangle of length 5 cm and breadth 2 cm

Step 1: Write the formula: Perimeter of rectangle = P = 2(ℓ + b)

Step 2: P = 2(5 + 2) = 2(7) = 14 cm.

Final answer: 14 cm

Worked examples — Exercise 8.1, Question 2: Find the area and perimeter of the following shapes

(i) Rectangle of length 6 cm and breadth 3 cm

Step 1: Write the formulae: Area of rectangle = ℓ × b and Perimeter of rectangle = 2(ℓ + b).

Step 2: Area = 6 × 3 = 18 cm².

Step 3: Perimeter = 2(6 + 3) = 2(9) = 18 cm.

Final answer: Area = 18 cm², Perimeter = 18 cm (Note: the book's Answers key prints P = 16 cm for this part; 2 × (6 + 3) = 18 cm.)

(ii) A grid figure made of squares of side 1 cm, 4 squares long and 4 squares wide (a 4 cm × 4 cm square)

Step 1: The whole figure is a square of side 4 × 1 cm = 4 cm.

Step 2: Write the formulae: Area of square = ℓ² and Perimeter of square = 4ℓ.

Step 3: Area = 4 × 4 = 16 cm² (also = 16 small squares of 1 cm²).

Step 4: Perimeter = 4 × 4 = 16 cm.

Final answer: Area = 16 cm², Perimeter = 16 cm

(iii) An L-shaped figure: total height 5 cm (3 cm + 2 cm), bottom side 8 cm, the step (notch) is 2 cm wide and the lower right part is 2 cm high

Step 1: Split the L into two rectangles: the upper left rectangle is (8 − 2) = 6 cm wide and 3 cm high; the lower rectangle is 8 cm long and 2 cm high.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of rectangle = ℓ × b. Area of upper part = 6 × 3 = 18 cm². Area of lower part = 8 × 2 = 16 cm².

Step 3: Total area = 18 + 16 = 34 cm².

Step 4: Perimeter = sum of all outer sides = 6 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 8 + 5 = 26 cm.

Final answer: Area = 34 cm², Perimeter = 26 cm (Note: the book's Answers key prints 14 cm² and 18 cm for this part, which matches a bottom side of 4 cm; the figure prints the bottom side as 8 cm, and the working above follows the printed figure.)

(iv) A cross (plus) figure made of 5 squares of side 1 cm each (bar width 1 cm; each arm 1 cm long)

Step 1: The cross is made of 5 equal squares, each of side 1 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of square = ℓ² = 1 × 1 = 1 cm² for one square. Total area = 5 × 1 = 5 cm².

Step 3: Perimeter: the boundary has 12 sides of 1 cm each, so perimeter = 12 × 1 = 12 cm.

Final answer: Area = 5 cm², Perimeter = 12 cm

Worked examples — Exercise 8.1, Questions 3 to 9

Q3. A rectangular certificate is 250 mm wide and 180 mm long. Find its area and perimeter.

Step 1: Length = 250 mm, breadth = 180 mm.

Step 2: Write the formulae: Area of rectangle = ℓ × b and Perimeter of rectangle = 2(ℓ + b).

Step 3: Area = 250 × 180 = 45,000 mm².

Step 4: Perimeter = 2(250 + 180) = 2(430) = 860 mm.

Final answer: Area = 45,000 mm², Perimeter = 860 mm

Q4. Find the length of each side of square painting if its perimeter is 49 m.

Step 1: Write the formula: Perimeter of square = P = 4ℓ, so side = P/4.

Step 2: Side = 49/4 = 12.25 m.

Final answer: Each side is 12.25 m.

Q5. The area of rectangle is 54 cm². If the breadth of rectangle is 6 cm, find its perimeter.

Step 1: Write the formula: Area of rectangle = ℓ × b, so length = Area / breadth = 54/6 = 9 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(ℓ + b) = 2(9 + 6) = 2(15) = 30 cm.

Final answer: Perimeter = 30 cm

Q6. Find the breadth of rectangle if its area is 60 cm² and length is 10 cm. Also find its perimeter.

Step 1: Write the formula: Breadth = Area of rectangle / Length = 60/10 = 6 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(ℓ + b) = 2(10 + 6) = 2(16) = 32 cm.

Final answer: Breadth = 6 cm, Perimeter = 32 cm

Q7. The perimeter of a square garden is 24 km. Find its area.

Step 1: Write the formula: Perimeter of square = 4ℓ, so side = 24/4 = 6 km.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of square = ℓ² = 6 × 6 = 36 km².

Final answer: Area = 36 km²

Q8. Zahid wants to grow plants in a square field. He plants 12 trees in a row. The cost of planting a tree is Rs. 100. How much money will be spent to plant the trees in the field?

Step 1: The field is square, with 12 trees in a row, so there are 12 rows of 12 trees.

Step 2: Total trees = 12 × 12 = 144.

Step 3: Cost = 144 × 100 = Rs. 14,400.

Final answer: Rs. 14,400 will be spent.

Q9. The length of rectangular field is 60 m and the breadth is 50 m. A girl wants to fence the field. The cost of fencing the field is Rs. 108 per metre. Find the total cost of fencing the field.

Step 1: Fencing is done around the boundary, so first find the perimeter. Write the formula: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(ℓ + b).

Step 2: Perimeter = 2(60 + 50) = 2(110) = 220 m.

Step 3: Total cost = 220 × 108 = Rs. 23,760.

Final answer: The total cost of fencing is Rs. 23,760. (Note: the book's Answers key prints Rs. 11000 for this question; the working above follows the printed length, breadth and rate.)

Worked examples — Exercise 8.1, Question 10: Find the area of the shaded parts of each shape

(i) A square of side 8 cm with an unshaded square hole inside it; the path (shaded border) is 1.5 cm wide

Step 1: Write the formula: Shaded area = Area of outer square − Area of inner square, with Area of square = ℓ².

Step 2: Area of outer square = 8 × 8 = 64 cm².

Step 3: Inner side = 8 − 1.5 − 1.5 = 5 cm. Area of inner square = 5 × 5 = 25 cm².

Step 4: Shaded area = 64 − 25 = 39 cm².

Final answer: 39 cm² (Note: the book's Answers key prints 96 cm² for this part, which is more than the whole 8 cm × 8 cm figure; the working above follows the printed figure.)

(ii) A rectangle 10 cm long, divided into horizontal strips of heights 2 cm, 1 cm and 2 cm; the top and bottom strips are fully shaded, and in the middle strip only a small 1 cm wide part is shaded

Step 1: Write the formula: Area of rectangle = ℓ × b.

Step 2: Top shaded strip = 10 × 2 = 20 cm². Bottom shaded strip = 10 × 2 = 20 cm².

Step 3: Middle shaded part = 1 × 1 = 1 cm².

Step 4: Total shaded area = 20 + 20 + 1 = 41 cm².

Final answer: 41 cm² (the small middle shaded part alone is 1 cm²)

(iii) A rectangle 14 cm long and 8 cm high, with an unshaded cross (paths) through it; the four shaded rectangles are each 3 cm high, and the vertical unshaded strip is 4 cm wide

Step 1: Width of each shaded rectangle = (14 − 4)/2 = 5 cm. Height of each shaded rectangle = 3 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of rectangle = ℓ × b. Area of one shaded rectangle = 5 × 3 = 15 cm².

Step 3: There are 4 equal shaded rectangles: total shaded area = 4 × 15 = 60 cm².

Final answer: 60 cm² (Note: the book's Answers key prints 24 cm² for this part; the working above follows the measurements printed in the figure.)

Worked examples — Exercise 8.1, Questions 11 and 12

Q11. A garden 100 m long and 50 m wide has a road 3 m wide all around the garden. Find the cost of paving the road at the rate of Rs. 250 per m².

Step 1: The road is all around the outside of the garden, so the outer length = 100 + 2 × 3 = 106 m and the outer breadth = 50 + 2 × 3 = 56 m.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of road = Area of outer rectangle − Area of garden, with Area of rectangle = ℓ × b.

Step 3: Area of outer rectangle = 106 × 56 = 5936 m². Area of garden = 100 × 50 = 5000 m².

Step 4: Area of road = 5936 − 5000 = 936 m².

Step 5: Cost of paving = 936 × 250 = Rs. 234,000.

Final answer: The cost of paving the road is Rs. 234,000. (Note: the book's Answers key prints Rs. 163500 for this question; the working above follows the printed garden size, road width and rate.)

Q12. In a square garden having each side of 25 m, two paths 6 m wide cross each other at right angle at the middle. Find the total area of the paths.

Step 1: Each path runs across the whole garden, so each path is 25 m long and 6 m wide.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of rectangle = ℓ × b. Area of one path = 25 × 6 = 150 m². Area of two paths = 2 × 150 = 300 m².

Step 3: The middle square, 6 m × 6 m = 36 m², where the paths cross, has been counted twice, so subtract it once: total area of paths = 300 − 36 = 264 m².

Final answer: The total area of the paths is 264 m².

mcqs.q: How is the area of a path around a rectangle found?
options: Area of large rectangle + area of small rectangle
Area of large rectangle − area of small rectangle
Perimeter of large rectangle − perimeter of small rectangle
mcqs.why: Area of path = area of large rectangle − area of small rectangle = (outer length × outer breadth) − (inner length × inner breadth).

mcqs.q: A path lies all around a park on the outside. What is the length of the park including the path?
options: Length of the park + 2 × width of the path
Length of the park + width of the path
Length of the park − 2 × width of the path
Length of the park × width of the path
mcqs.why: The path adds its width on both ends of the park, so length including the path = length of the park + 2 × width of the path.

mcqs.q: In Example 8, the outer measurement (park with path) is 80 m by 50 m. What is the area of the park with the path?
mcqs.why: Area of a rectangle: A = outer length × outer breadth. Working: A₁ = 80 × 50 = 4000 m², as solved in Example 8.

mcqs.q: In Example 8, the path is 4 m wide and the outer length is 80 m. What is the inner length of the park?
mcqs.why: The path takes 4 m from both ends, so inner length = 80 − (2 × 4) = 80 − 8 = 72 m, as worked in Example 8.

mcqs.q: In Example 8, the area with the path is 4000 m² and the area of the park without the path is 3024 m². What is the area of the path?
mcqs.why: Area of path = A₁ − A₂, where each area uses A = length × breadth. Working: 4000 − 3024 = 976 m², from Example 8.

mcqs.q: In Example 8, the area of the path is 976 m² and turfing costs Rs. 200 per m². What is the cost of turfing the path?
mcqs.why: Area of path = 4000 − 3024 = 976 m² (using A = length × breadth for both rectangles). Cost = 200 × 976 = Rs. 195,200.

mcqs.q: A garden is 100 m long and a road 3 m wide runs all around the outside of it. What is the outer length including the road?
mcqs.why: For an outside path, outer length = length of the garden + 2 × width of the road = 100 + 2 × 3 = 106 m.

mcqs.q: A garden 100 m by 50 m has a road 3 m wide all around the outside. Find the area of the road.
mcqs.why: Area of road = outer area − garden area, with A = ℓ × b. Outer area = 106 × 56 = 5936 m²; garden area = 100 × 50 = 5000 m²; road = 5936 − 5000 = 936 m².

mcqs.q: In a square garden of side 25 m, two paths 6 m wide cross each other at right angles in the middle. Find the total area of the paths.
mcqs.why: Area of one path = ℓ × b = 25 × 6 = 150 m², so two paths = 300 m². The middle 6 × 6 = 36 m² square is counted twice, so total = 300 − 36 = 264 m².

mcqs.q: A square of side 8 cm has an unshaded square hole inside it and the shaded border (path) is 1.5 cm wide. Find the shaded area.
mcqs.why: Shaded area = outer area − inner area, with A = ℓ². Outer area = 8 × 8 = 64 cm²; inner side = 8 − 1.5 − 1.5 = 5 cm, inner area = 25 cm²; shaded = 64 − 25 = 39 cm². The book's key prints 96 cm², which is impossible as it exceeds the whole 64 cm² figure.

lessons.title: 8.1.4 Altitude of Geometrical Figure
lessons.notes_html:
Altitude of a geometrical figure

The word altitude means the height of an object above a reference level or sea level, i.e. when we are in an aeroplane, the attendant probably updates us that how high up the aeroplane is in the air. This is known as altitude of the aeroplane. This altitude refers to how high the aeroplane is with respect to sea level. In geometry: “The altitude is measured of the shortest distance between the base and its top.”

The book shows the altitude drawn as a perpendicular line from the top of a triangle, a parallelogram and a trapezium down to the base, marked with a right-angle sign at the base.

Example 9 — Identify the altitudes of the following geometrical shapes

(i) In the first figure (two joined shapes on base AB, with perpendiculars DE and BF drawn to the base line): the segments drawn at right angle to the base are DE and BF.

Final answer: (i) The altitudes are mDE and mBF (as printed in the book's solution).

(ii) In the second figure (joined shapes on base AJ, with perpendiculars BC, DE and HT): the segments drawn at right angle to the base are BC, DE and HT.

Final answer: (ii) The altitudes are mBC, mDE and mHT (as printed in the book's solution).

mcqs.q: In everyday language, what does the word altitude mean?
options: The region enclosed by an object
The height of an object above a reference level or sea level
The length of the longest side of an object
mcqs.why: The lesson explains that altitude means the height of an object above a reference level or sea level, like the height of an aeroplane.

mcqs.q: When an aeroplane attendant announces the altitude, what does it refer to?
options: How high the aeroplane is with respect to sea level
How fast the aeroplane is flying
How far the aeroplane has travelled
How many passengers the aeroplane is carrying
mcqs.why: The lesson's aeroplane example says this altitude refers to how high the aeroplane is with respect to sea level.

mcqs.q: In geometry, how is the altitude measured?
options: As the distance around the base
As the shortest distance between the base and its top
As the longest distance across the figure
As the sum of all the sides of the figure
mcqs.why: The lesson defines the altitude in geometry as measured of the shortest distance between the base and its top of a figure.

mcqs.q: How is the altitude drawn in the book's figures of a triangle, a parallelogram and a trapezium?
options: As a curved line from the top
As a diagonal line across the figure
As a line along the top side
As a perpendicular line from the top down to the base
mcqs.why: The book shows the altitude drawn as a perpendicular line from the top of each figure down to the base, with a right-angle sign at the base.

mcqs.q: What mark is shown at the base where the altitude meets it?
mcqs.why: The altitude is perpendicular to the base, and the book marks this with a right-angle sign at the base in its figures.

mcqs.q: For a trapezium, where does the altitude line end?
options: Along the top side of the trapezium
Only at a corner of the trapezium
mcqs.why: Like the triangle and parallelogram shown, the trapezium's altitude is drawn as a perpendicular line from its top down to its base.

mcqs.q: In Example 9(i), two joined shapes stand on base AB, with perpendiculars DE and BF drawn to the base line. What are the altitudes?
mcqs.why: The segments drawn at right angle to the base are the altitudes; in Example 9(i) these are DE and BF, written as mDE and mBF.

mcqs.q: In Example 9(ii), joined shapes stand on base AJ, with perpendiculars BC, DE and HT drawn. What are the altitudes?
mcqs.why: The segments drawn at right angle to the base AJ are BC, DE and HT, so the altitudes are mBC, mDE and mHT, as in Example 9(ii).

mcqs.q: A segment in a figure counts as an altitude when it is drawn in which way?
options: As any slanted segment in the figure
As any side of the figure
As a segment parallel to the base
As a segment at right angle to the base
mcqs.why: In Example 9 only the segments drawn at right angle (perpendicular) to the base are identified as the altitudes of the figures.

mcqs.q: Between which two parts of a figure is the altitude measured?
options: Between the base and its top
Between the centre and a corner
mcqs.why: The geometry definition measures the altitude as the shortest distance between the base and its top, drawn perpendicular to the base.

lessons.title: 8.1.5 Area of Parallelogram
lessons.notes_html:
Parallelogram

A parallelogram is a 4-sided plane figure formed by two pairs of parallel lines. Opposite sides are equal in length and opposite angles are equal in measurement. The height is fixed. In a parallelogram, when we draw a perpendicular from any point of its opposite side, then this perpendicular is known as height and the opposite side is known as its base.

Remember: The altitude always makes the right angle with the base. Altitude of a parallelogram is also known as perpendicular height of a parallelogram.

Area of a parallelogram

To find the area of parallelogram, consider a parallelogram PQRS. A perpendicular QT is drawn on the base PS, so a triangle PQT is formed. The triangular area is cut from QT and placed with RS, and we get a rectangle TQRT′. The above activity shows that a parallelogram can be converted into a rectangle. So, the area of rectangle and area of parallelogram is same and we can use the same formula:

Area of rectangle = Area of parallelogram; Length × breadth = mPS × mQT. Here, the line segment mQT is the “altitude” of the parallelogram PQRS, and mPS is the base. So, the area of parallelogram = base × altitude. If we represent base of parallelogram with “b” and altitude with “a”, then A = b × a.

Area of a parallelogram = base × perpendicular height (A = b × h)

Example 10 — Find the area of a parallelogram if its base is 12 cm and perpendicular height is 8 cm

Step 1: Base of parallelogram = b = 12 cm, perpendicular height of parallelogram = h = 8 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of parallelogram = base × perpendicular height (A = b × h)

Step 3: A = 12 × 8 = 96 cm².

Final answer: The area of the parallelogram is 96 cm².

Example 11 — The area of parallelogram is 144 cm², and the base of parallelogram is 18 cm. Find the height of parallelogram.

Step 1: Base of parallelogram = b = 18 cm, area of parallelogram = A = 144 cm².

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of a parallelogram = base × perpendicular height (A = b × h), so h = A/b.

Step 3: h = 144/18 = 8 cm.

Final answer: The height of the parallelogram is 8 cm.

Worked example — Practice-2

Calculate the area of parallelogram if its length (base) is 13 cm and altitude is 9 cm.

Step 1: Base = 13 cm, altitude (perpendicular height) = 9 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of parallelogram = base × perpendicular height

Step 3: Area = 13 × 9 = 117 cm².

Final answer: 117 cm²

Perimeter of parallelogram

“The total length of the boundaries or all sides of a parallelogram is called its perimeter.” The perimeter of parallelogram is same as the perimeter of rectangle as both shapes have the same properties. Let “a” and “b” be the length of sides of the parallelogram. We know that the opposite sides of parallelogram are equal. So we can calculate the perimeter of parallelogram by using the formula:

Perimeter of parallelogram: P = (a + b + a + b) = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b)

Example 12 — Find the perimeter of the parallelogram, whose dimensions are 12 cm and 6 cm

Step 1: Base of parallelogram = 12 cm, side length of parallelogram = 6 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Perimeter of parallelogram = P = 2(a + b)

Step 3: P = 2(12 + 6) = 2(18) = 36 cm.

Final answer: The required perimeter of the parallelogram is 36 cm.

Worked example — Practice-3

Calculate the perimeter of the parallelogram, whose dimensions are 11 m and 7 m respectively.

Step 1: The two side lengths are a = 11 m and b = 7 m.

Step 2: Write the formula: Perimeter of parallelogram = 2(a + b)

Step 3: Perimeter = 2(11 + 7) = 2(18) = 36 m.

Final answer: 36 m

mcqs.q: What is a parallelogram?
options: A 4-sided plane figure formed by two pairs of parallel lines
A 3-sided plane figure with equal sides
A round plane figure with no sides
mcqs.why: The lesson defines a parallelogram as a 4-sided plane figure formed by two pairs of parallel lines, with a fixed height.

mcqs.q: Which statement about a parallelogram is correct?
options: Its opposite sides are always unequal
Only one of its sides is equal to another
All of its angles are right angles
Opposite sides are equal in length and opposite angles are equal in measurement
mcqs.why: The lesson states that in a parallelogram opposite sides are equal in length and opposite angles are equal in measurement.

mcqs.q: In a parallelogram, a perpendicular is drawn from any point of one side to the opposite side. What are these called?
options: The perpendicular is the base and the side is the height
The perpendicular is the height and the opposite side is the base
mcqs.why: The lesson says this perpendicular is known as the height and the opposite side it meets is known as the base of the parallelogram.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the altitude of a parallelogram is correct?
options: It makes an acute angle with the base
It runs parallel to the base
It always makes a right angle with the base
It is always equal to the base
mcqs.why: The lesson reminds us that the altitude always makes the right angle with the base, and it is also called the perpendicular height.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the area of a parallelogram?
mcqs.why: Area of a parallelogram = base × perpendicular height, written A = b × h, the same form as the rectangle it can be converted into.

mcqs.q: Why can the rectangle's formula be used for a parallelogram's area?
options: Because a parallelogram is a circle in disguise
Because its area becomes double the rectangle's area
Because a parallelogram can be converted into a rectangle with the same area
mcqs.why: In the PQRS activity the triangular part cut along altitude QT is placed with RS to form rectangle TQRT′, showing both areas are the same.

mcqs.q: Find the area of a parallelogram if its base is 12 cm and its perpendicular height is 8 cm.
mcqs.why: Area of a parallelogram: A = b × h (base × perpendicular height). Working: A = 12 × 8 = 96 cm², which is Example 10.

mcqs.q: The area of a parallelogram is 144 cm² and its base is 18 cm. Find its height.
mcqs.why: Area of a parallelogram: A = b × h, so h = A / b. Working: h = 144 / 18 = 8 cm, which is Example 11 of this lesson.

mcqs.q: Calculate the area of a parallelogram if its base is 13 cm and its altitude is 9 cm.
mcqs.why: Area of a parallelogram = base × perpendicular height (altitude). Working: Area = 13 × 9 = 117 cm², from Practice-2 of this lesson.

mcqs.q: Find the perimeter of a parallelogram whose dimensions are 12 cm and 6 cm.
mcqs.why: Perimeter of a parallelogram: P = 2(a + b), since opposite sides are equal. Working: P = 2(12 + 6) = 2(18) = 36 cm, from Example 12.

lessons.title: 8.1.6 Area of a Trapezium
lessons.notes_html:
Trapezium

A trapezium is a quadrilateral with four sides and four angles. It has only two parallel sides. The trapezium is also known as trapezoid. There are three kinds of trapezium:

  • Isosceles trapezium: If the non-parallel sides of a trapezium are equal in length then the trapezium is called isosceles trapezium.
  • Scalene trapezium: If all the sides and all the angles of a trapezium are of different measurement then the trapezium is called scalene trapezium.
  • Right trapezium: If a trapezium has two right angles then the trapezium is called right trapezium.

Remember — Regular Trapezium: A trapezium whose non-parallel sides are equal in length and its base angles are equal is known as regular trapezium.

Area of trapezium

To find the area of trapezium, we consider two congruent trapeziums with perpendicular height h and the opposite (parallel) sides S₁ and S₂ respectively. Now, put the above two trapeziums together to form a parallelogram (we can form a parallelogram by rotating the original trapezium at 180°). As, Area of parallelogram = base × perpendicular height = b × h = (S₁ + S₂) × perpendicular height. The area of original trapezium is one half of the area of the parallelogram. So:

Area of trapezium = (1/2)(side₁ + side₂) × perpendicular height, i.e. A = (1/2)(S₁ + S₂) × h

Example 13 — Find the area of trapezium whose length of parallel sides is 10 cm and 12 cm respectively, with perpendicular height 8 cm

Step 1: Longer base of trapezium = S₁ = 12 cm, shorter base of trapezium = S₂ = 10 cm, height of trapezium = h = 8 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of trapezium = (1/2)(side₁ + side₂) × perpendicular height = (1/2)(S₁ + S₂) × h

Step 3: Substitute: Area = (1/2)(12 + 10) × 8 = (1/2)(22) × 8 = 88 cm².

Final answer: The area of the trapezium is 88 cm².

Worked example — Practice-4

Find the area of trapezium whose length of parallel sides is 15 cm and 12 cm respectively, its perpendicular height is 6 cm.

Step 1: Parallel sides are 15 cm and 12 cm; perpendicular height = 6 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of trapezium = (1/2)(S₁ + S₂) × h

Step 3: Area = (1/2)(15 + 12) × 6 = (1/2)(27) × 6 = 81 cm².

Final answer: 81 cm²

Perimeter of trapezium

“The sum of all sides of a trapezium is called its perimeter.” Perimeter can be calculated by using the formula:

Perimeter of trapezium = P = a + b + c + d, where a, b, c and d are the length of sides of the trapezium.

Example 14 — If the lengths of parallel sides of a trapezium are 15 cm and 10 cm, and non-parallel sides are 6 cm each. Find its perimeter.

Step 1: Lengths of parallel sides = 15 cm and 10 cm; lengths of non-parallel sides = 6 cm each.

Step 2: Write the formula: Perimeter of trapezium = P = a + b + c + d

Step 3: P = 15 + 6 + 10 + 6 = 21 + 16 = 37 cm.

Final answer: The perimeter of the trapezium is 37 cm.

Worked example — Practice-5

What is the perimeter of trapezium ABCD? If mAB = 20 cm, mBC = 4 cm, mCD = 13 cm and mAD = 5 cm.

Step 1: The four sides are 20 cm, 4 cm, 13 cm and 5 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Perimeter of trapezium = P = a + b + c + d

Step 3: P = 20 + 4 + 13 + 5 = 42 cm.

Final answer: 42 cm

mcqs.q: What is a trapezium?
options: A quadrilateral whose all four sides are parallel in pairs
A quadrilateral with four sides and four angles which has only two parallel sides
A quadrilateral with no parallel sides at all
A quadrilateral with four equal sides and four right angles
mcqs.why: The notes define a trapezium as a quadrilateral with four sides and four angles, and it has only two parallel sides.

mcqs.q: A trapezium is also known by which other name?
mcqs.why: The notes state directly that the trapezium is also known as trapezoid.

mcqs.q: When is a trapezium called an isosceles trapezium?
options: When its non-parallel sides are equal in length
When all its sides and angles are different
When it has two right angles
When its parallel sides are equal in length
mcqs.why: The notes say: if the non-parallel sides of a trapezium are equal in length, the trapezium is called an isosceles trapezium.

mcqs.q: What is a scalene trapezium?
options: A trapezium with two right angles
A trapezium whose non-parallel sides are equal
A trapezium whose base angles are equal
A trapezium in which all the sides and all the angles are of different measurement
mcqs.why: The notes define a scalene trapezium as one in which all the sides and all the angles are of different measurement.

mcqs.q: A right trapezium is a trapezium that has:
mcqs.why: The notes state: if a trapezium has two right angles, then the trapezium is called a right trapezium.

mcqs.q: A regular trapezium is a trapezium whose:
options: All sides and all angles are different
Parallel sides are equal and it has two right angles
Non-parallel sides are equal in length and its base angles are equal
Only one pair of sides is unequal
mcqs.why: The notes say a trapezium whose non-parallel sides are equal in length and whose base angles are equal is known as a regular trapezium.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the area of a trapezium with parallel sides S1 and S2 and perpendicular height h?
mcqs.why: Two congruent trapeziums form a parallelogram of area (S1 + S2) x h, so one trapezium has half of it: A = (1/2)(S1 + S2) x h.

mcqs.q: Find the area of a trapezium whose parallel sides are 10 cm and 12 cm, with perpendicular height 8 cm.
Find the area of a trapezium whose parallel sides are 15 cm and 12 cm, with perpendicular height 6 cm.
The parallel sides of a trapezium are 15 cm and 10 cm, and the non-parallel sides are 6 cm each. What is its perimeter?
mcqs.why: Formula: Perimeter of trapezium P = a + b + c + d (sum of all sides). Working: P = 15 + 6 + 10 + 6 = 37 cm.

lessons.title: 8.1.7 Area of Triangle
lessons.notes_html:
Triangle

We know about triangle that it is a polygon having three sides and three angles. In previous classes we have learnt about different types of triangle such as, equilateral, isosceles, scalene and right angled triangle.

Area of a triangle

Consider a parallelogram PQRS which is divided into two equal triangles, PQS and QRS. As, Area of parallelogram = base × perpendicular height. So, the area of the triangle PQS is half the area of parallelogram. Similarly, the area of the triangle QRS is also half the area of parallelogram.

Area of triangle = (1/2) × base × height, i.e. A = (1/2)(b × h). This formula can also be used for other triangles.

Remember: The height of the triangle is always measured at right angle to the base.

Example 15 — Find the area of the triangle having base length 12 cm and the height 8 cm

Step 1: Base length of triangle = b = 12 cm, perpendicular height of triangle = h = 8 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of triangle = (1/2) × base × height = (1/2)(b × h)

Step 3: Area = (1/2)(12 × 8) = 96/2 = 48 cm².

Final answer: The area of the triangle is 48 cm².

Worked example — Practice-6

Find the area of triangle ABC having base length 9 cm and its perpendicular height 5 cm.

Step 1: Base = 9 cm, perpendicular height = 5 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of triangle = (1/2) × base × height

Step 3: Area = (1/2)(9 × 5) = 45/2 = 22.5 cm².

Final answer: 22.5 cm²

Perimeter of a triangle

“The sum of all sides of a triangle is called its perimeter.” To calculate the perimeter of any triangle we use the formula:

Perimeter of triangle = P = a + b + c, where a, b and c are the length of all sides of given triangle.

Example 16 — Find the perimeter of triangle ABC having lengths of sides 6 cm, 7 cm and 8 cm respectively

Step 1: Length of mAB = 6 cm, length of mBC = 7 cm, length of mAC = 8 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Perimeter of triangle = P = mAB + mBC + mAC

Step 3: P = 6 + 7 + 8 = 21 cm.

Final answer: The required perimeter of the triangle is 21 cm.

Worked example — Practice-7

Find the length of missing side of triangle whose perimeter is 36 cm and two sides are 10 cm and 11 cm respectively.

Step 1: Write the formula: Perimeter of triangle = P = a + b + c, so the missing side = Perimeter − (sum of the two known sides).

Step 2: Missing side = 36 − (10 + 11) = 36 − 21 = 15 cm.

Final answer: 15 cm

Worked examples — Exercise 8.2, Question 1: Identify the altitudes of the following figures

Rule: the altitude is the segment drawn at right angle (perpendicular) to the base.

(i) Triangle ABF, with segments BC, BD and BE from B to the base AF; only BC carries the right-angle mark at C.

Final answer: The altitude is BC.

(ii) Triangle PQR, with RS drawn at right angle to base PQ at S, and PT drawn at right angle to side RQ at T.

Final answer: The altitudes are RS and PT.

(iii) Parallelogram ABCD (A and B on the base, D and C on the top), with DF drawn from D perpendicular to the base at F, and EB drawn from E on the top side perpendicular to the base at B.

Final answer: The altitudes are DF and EB. (Note: the book's Answers key prints “AF and CE” for this part; AF and CE are parts of the base and top sides in the printed figure, while the perpendicular segments are DF and EB.)

Worked examples — Exercise 8.2, Question 2: Calculate the area and perimeter for each of these parallelograms, trapeziums and triangles

Note: In each figure below, the lengths of the slanted sides are not printed, so the perimeter cannot be completed from the figure; the area is calculated in full (the book's Answers key also gives only the area for this question).

(i) Parallelogram with base 3 cm and altitude (perpendicular height) 8 cm

Step 1: Base = 3 cm, perpendicular height = 8 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of parallelogram = base × perpendicular height

Step 3: Area = 3 × 8 = 24 cm².

Final answer: Area = 24 cm² (perimeter cannot be found: the slanted side is not given)

(ii) Parallelogram with base 10 cm and altitude (perpendicular height) 5 cm

Step 1: Base = 10 cm, perpendicular height = 5 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of parallelogram = base × perpendicular height

Step 3: Area = 10 × 5 = 50 cm².

Final answer: Area = 50 cm² (perimeter cannot be found: the slanted side is not given)

(iii) Trapezium with parallel sides 4 cm and 8 cm and perpendicular height 3 cm

Step 1: Parallel sides S₁ = 8 cm, S₂ = 4 cm; height h = 3 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of trapezium = (1/2)(S₁ + S₂) × h

Step 3: Area = (1/2)(8 + 4) × 3 = (1/2)(12) × 3 = 18 cm².

Final answer: Area = 18 cm² (perimeter cannot be found: the non-parallel sides are not given)

(iv) Right trapezium with parallel sides 3 cm and 7 cm and the distance between them (base) 5 cm

Step 1: Parallel sides are 3 cm and 7 cm; perpendicular height = 5 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of trapezium = (1/2)(S₁ + S₂) × h

Step 3: Area = (1/2)(3 + 7) × 5 = (1/2)(10) × 5 = 25 cm².

Final answer: Area = 25 cm² (perimeter cannot be found: the slanted side is not given)

(v) Triangle with base 6 cm and height 4 cm

Step 1: Base = 6 cm, height = 4 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of triangle = (1/2) × base × height

Step 3: Area = (1/2)(6 × 4) = 24/2 = 12 cm².

Final answer: Area = 12 cm² (perimeter cannot be found: the other sides are not given)

(vi) Triangle with base 10 cm, altitude 4 cm and one side 5 cm

Step 1: Base = 10 cm, altitude (perpendicular height) = 4 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Area of triangle = (1/2) × base × height

Step 3: Area = (1/2)(10 × 4) = 40/2 = 20 cm².

Final answer: Area = 20 cm² (perimeter cannot be found: only one other side, 5 cm, is given. Note: the book's Answers key prints 25 cm² for this part, which uses 5 cm as the height; the figure labels the dashed altitude as 4 cm.)

Worked examples — Exercise 8.2, Question 3: Find the area of each shaded shape

(i) A shaded trapezium (parallel sides 4 cm and 8 cm, height 4 cm) joined to a shaded parallelogram below it (base 8 cm, height 3 cm)

Step 1: Write the formulae: Area of trapezium = (1/2)(S₁ + S₂) × h and Area of parallelogram = base × perpendicular height.

Step 2: Area of trapezium = (1/2)(4 + 8) × 4 = (1/2)(12) × 4 = 24 cm².

Step 3: Area of parallelogram = 8 × 3 = 24 cm².

Step 4: Total shaded area = 24 + 24 = 48 cm².

Final answer: 48 cm²

(ii) A shaded composite shape of total width 8 cm: a top triangle (base 4 cm, height 5 cm), a middle trapezium (parallel sides 4 cm and 8 cm, height 6 cm) and a bottom rectangle (8 cm by 2 cm)

Step 1: Write the formulae: Area of triangle = (1/2) × base × height, Area of trapezium = (1/2)(S₁ + S₂) × h and Area of rectangle = ℓ × b.

Step 2: Area of top triangle = (1/2)(4 × 5) = 10 cm².

Step 3: Area of middle trapezium = (1/2)(4 + 8) × 6 = (1/2)(12) × 6 = 36 cm².

Step 4: Area of bottom rectangle = 8 × 2 = 16 cm².

Step 5: Total shaded area = 10 + 36 + 16 = 62 cm².

Final answer: 62 cm² (Note: the book's Answers key prints 57 cm² for this part; the working above follows the measurements printed in the figure.)

(iii) A shaded trapezium inside a 10 cm by 7 cm rectangle, with parallel sides 4 cm and 10 cm and height 7 cm

Step 1: Write the formula: Area of trapezium = (1/2)(S₁ + S₂) × h

Step 2: Area = (1/2)(4 + 10) × 7 = (1/2)(14) × 7 = 49 cm².

Final answer: 49 cm²

Worked examples — Exercise 8.2, Questions 4 to 8

Q4. The area of a parallelogram is 126 cm² and its perpendicular height is 9 cm. Find its base. Also, calculate its perimeter.

Step 1: Write the formula: Area of parallelogram = base × perpendicular height, so base = Area / perpendicular height.

Step 2: Base = 126/9 = 14 cm.

Step 3: The perimeter needs the slanted side length, which is not given, so the perimeter cannot be calculated from the given information (the book's Answers key also gives only the base, 14 cm).

Final answer: Base = 14 cm; perimeter cannot be found from the given data.

Q5. The base and area of parallelogram is 9 cm and 99 cm² respectively. Find its perpendicular height.

Step 1: Write the formula: Area of parallelogram = base × perpendicular height, so height = Area / base.

Step 2: Height = 99/9 = 11 cm.

Final answer: Perpendicular height = 11 cm

Q6. The parallel sides of a trapezium are 25 cm and 30 cm and its area is 192.5 cm². What is the height of trapezium?

Step 1: Write the formula: Area of trapezium = (1/2)(S₁ + S₂) × h

Step 2: 192.5 = (1/2)(25 + 30) × h = (1/2)(55) × h = 27.5 × h.

Step 3: h = 192.5/27.5 = 7 cm.

Final answer: Height = 7 cm

Q7. A trapezium has a longer base that is 25 cm and the height is 5 cm. The area of trapezium is 200 cm². What is the shorter base of the trapezium?

Step 1: Write the formula: Area of trapezium = (1/2)(S₁ + S₂) × h. Let the shorter base = S₂.

Step 2: 200 = (1/2)(25 + S₂) × 5.

Step 3: Multiply both sides by 2: 400 = (25 + S₂) × 5.

Step 4: Divide both sides by 5: 80 = 25 + S₂.

Step 5: S₂ = 80 − 25 = 55 cm.

Final answer: Shorter base = 55 cm

Q8. The height of a triangular garden is 55 m and base is 90 m. Find the number of flowers in the garden if 20 flowers are in the area of each square metre.

Step 1: Write the formula: Area of triangle = (1/2) × base × height

Step 2: Area of garden = (1/2)(90 × 55) = (1/2)(4950) = 2475 m².

Step 3: Number of flowers = 2475 × 20 = 49,500.

Final answer: 49,500 flowers

mcqs.q: A triangle is a polygon having:
mcqs.why: The notes state that a triangle is a polygon having three sides and three angles.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the area of a triangle with base b and height h?
mcqs.why: A parallelogram is divided into two equal triangles, so each triangle has half its area: Area of triangle = (1/2) x base x height, i.e. A = (1/2)(b x h).

mcqs.q: Why is the area of a triangle half the area of a parallelogram?
options: Because a triangle has only three sides
Because a parallelogram is divided into two equal triangles, so each triangle is half of the parallelogram
Because the height of a triangle is half the height of a parallelogram
Because the base of a triangle is doubled in a parallelogram
mcqs.why: The notes divide parallelogram PQRS into two equal triangles PQS and QRS, so the area of each triangle is half the area of the parallelogram.

mcqs.q: How is the height of a triangle always measured?
options: Along any slanted side of the triangle
At right angle to the base
mcqs.why: The notes remind us that the height of the triangle is always measured at right angle to the base.

mcqs.q: Find the area of a triangle having base length 12 cm and height 8 cm.
mcqs.why: Formula: Area = (1/2) x base x height. Working: Area = (1/2)(12 x 8) = 96/2 = 48 cm^2.

mcqs.q: Find the area of triangle ABC having base length 9 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm.
mcqs.why: Formula: Area = (1/2) x base x height. Working: Area = (1/2)(9 x 5) = 45/2 = 22.5 cm^2.

mcqs.q: Find the perimeter of triangle ABC having sides 6 cm, 7 cm and 8 cm.
mcqs.why: Formula: Perimeter of triangle P = a + b + c, the sum of all sides. Working: P = 6 + 7 + 8 = 21 cm.

mcqs.q: The perimeter of a triangle is 36 cm and two of its sides are 10 cm and 11 cm. What is the length of the missing side?
mcqs.why: Formula: P = a + b + c, so missing side = Perimeter - (sum of known sides). Working: 36 - (10 + 11) = 36 - 21 = 15 cm.

mcqs.q: A triangle has base 10 cm and altitude 4 cm (one other side is 5 cm). What is its area?
mcqs.why: Formula: Area = (1/2) x base x height, using the altitude 4 cm, not the side 5 cm. Working: (1/2)(10 x 4) = 40/2 = 20 cm^2. The book key's 25 cm^2 wrongly uses 5 cm as the height.

mcqs.q: A triangular garden has base 90 m and height 55 m. If 20 flowers grow in each square metre, how many flowers are in the garden?
mcqs.why: Formula: Area = (1/2) x base x height = (1/2)(90 x 55) = 2475 m^2. Working: number of flowers = 2475 x 20 = 49,500 flowers.

lessons.title: 8.2 3-Dimensional Shapes/Figures (Cube and Cuboid)
lessons.notes_html:
3-Dimensional shapes/figures

The solid figures are 3-dimensional figures. These figures have height, width and depth. All solid figures have thickness and can be held in our hand. For example, cube, cuboid etc.

mcqs.q: Solid figures are also called:
options: Figures with only height and width
mcqs.why: The notes begin: the solid figures are 3-dimensional figures, so solid figures and 3-dimensional figures are the same thing.

mcqs.q: Which three measurements do 3-dimensional figures have, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes state that these figures have height, width and depth - all three measurements together.

mcqs.q: Besides height and width, which third measurement does a solid figure have?
mcqs.why: The notes list the measurements of solid figures as height, width and depth, so the third one named is depth.

mcqs.q: What do all solid figures have, in addition to height, width and depth?
options: They have thickness only on one side
They have thickness in some cases
mcqs.why: The notes state clearly: all solid figures have thickness, with no exception mentioned.

mcqs.q: What can be done with solid figures because they are solid?
options: They can be held in our hand
They can only be drawn on paper
They can only be seen, not touched
mcqs.why: The notes state that solid figures can be held in our hand, which is one of their stated features.

mcqs.q: Which pair of figures is given in the notes as examples of solid figures?
mcqs.why: The notes end with the examples 'cube, cuboid etc.', so both cube and cuboid are given as examples of solid figures.

mcqs.q: A cube is an example of which kind of figure?
options: A figure that cannot be held in the hand
A figure with only height and width
mcqs.why: The notes give the cube as an example of a solid figure, and solid figures are 3-dimensional figures.

mcqs.q: A cuboid is an example of which kind of figure?
options: A figure with only width and depth
A figure that cannot be held in the hand
mcqs.why: The notes give the cuboid as an example of a solid figure, and solid figures are 3-dimensional figures.

mcqs.q: Which statement matches the notes about solid figures?
options: Solid figures have thickness and can be held in our hand
Solid figures have thickness but cannot be held in our hand
Solid figures can be held in our hand but have no thickness
Solid figures have neither thickness nor can they be held
mcqs.why: The notes state both facts together: all solid figures have thickness and can be held in our hand.

mcqs.q: Which description best fits a solid figure as described in the notes?
options: It has height and width but no depth
It has depth but no thickness
It has height, width and depth, and it has thickness
It has thickness but no height, width or depth
mcqs.why: The notes describe solid figures as having height, width and depth, and also state that all solid figures have thickness.

lessons.title: 8.2.1 Units of Surface Area and Volume
lessons.notes_html:
Surface area

We have learnt about area and perimeter in our previous section. The area of any 2-dimensional figure or shape is the measurement of space occupied by the figure, such as a unit square (1 cm by 1 cm) has the area of 1 square unit.

Similarly, the surface area of any three-dimensional solid figure is the sum of the areas of all of its faces. It is also measured in square units. For example a cube has 6 faces. If the area of each face is 1 cm² then the surface area of cube will be the sum of area of all its faces i.e. 1 cm² + 1 cm² + 1 cm² + 1 cm² + 1 cm² + 1 cm² = 6 cm².

Volume

“The volume is the quantity of three dimensional space enclosed by a closed surface.”

The volume of the solid figure like cube or cuboid is the number of cubic units that it contains. The cubic units may be cubic centimetres or cubic metres and so on. If one side length of cube is 1 cm then its volume will be 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm = 1 cm³.

Remember: Most of the time the dimensions of cube or cuboid are given in different units. They will be converted into the same unit before calculating the volume and surface area.

mcqs.q: The area of any 2-dimensional figure or shape is:
options: The measurement of space occupied by the figure
The sum of the areas of all its faces
The number of cubic units it contains
mcqs.why: The notes state that the area of any 2-dimensional figure is the measurement of space occupied by the figure.

mcqs.q: A unit square of 1 cm by 1 cm has an area of:
mcqs.why: The notes give this example: a unit square (1 cm by 1 cm) has the area of 1 square unit.

mcqs.q: The surface area of a three-dimensional solid figure is:
options: The sum of the areas of all of its faces
The area of its largest face only
The quantity of space enclosed by it
mcqs.why: The notes define surface area as the sum of the areas of all the faces of a three-dimensional solid figure.

mcqs.q: In which units is surface area measured?
mcqs.why: The notes state that surface area is measured in square units, just like the area of a flat figure.

mcqs.q: A cube has 6 faces and the area of each face is 1 cm^2. What is the surface area of the cube?
mcqs.why: Surface area is the sum of the areas of all faces. Working: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6 cm^2 for the 6 faces.

mcqs.q: Volume is defined in the notes as:
options: The sum of the areas of all faces of a solid
The distance around a closed shape
The quantity of three dimensional space enclosed by a closed surface
The number of faces of a solid figure
mcqs.why: The notes define volume word for word as the quantity of three dimensional space enclosed by a closed surface.

mcqs.q: The volume of a solid figure like a cube or cuboid is:
options: The number of cubic units that it contains
The number of square units on its faces
The sum of its edge lengths
The area of one of its faces
mcqs.why: The notes state that the volume of a solid figure like a cube or cuboid is the number of cubic units that it contains.

mcqs.q: Which of these are units of volume mentioned in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes say the cubic units may be cubic centimetres or cubic metres, so volume is measured in cubic units.

mcqs.q: What is the volume of a cube with side length 1 cm?
mcqs.why: Formula: Volume = length x length x length. Working: 1 cm x 1 cm x 1 cm = 1 cm^3, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: If the dimensions of a cube or cuboid are given in different units, what must be done before calculating volume and surface area?
options: They are used as they are, without any change
Only the largest unit is kept and the rest are dropped
They are converted into the same unit first
They are all converted into kilometres
mcqs.why: The notes remind us that dimensions given in different units are converted into the same unit before calculating the volume and surface area.

lessons.title: 8.2.2 Find Surface Area and Volume of Cube and Cuboid
lessons.notes_html:
Surface area of cube

In the cube, the length, breadth and height are same: length = breadth = height. The surface area of cube can be calculated by using the formula:

Surface area of cube = 6 × (length × length) = 6 × (length)² = 6ℓ²

Example 17 — The figure shows a cube with 8 cm long each side. Find the total surface area of the figure.

Step 1: Length of each side of cube = ℓ = 8 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Surface area of cube = 6ℓ²

Step 3: Surface area = 6(8)² = 6 × 64 = 384 cm².

Final answer: The required surface area of cube is 384 cm².

Worked example — Practice-8

Use formula to find the surface area of cube having length of each side 10 cm.

Step 1: ℓ = 10 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Surface area of cube = 6ℓ²

Step 3: Surface area = 6(10)² = 6 × 100 = 600 cm².

Final answer: 600 cm²

Surface area of cuboid

We are familiar that in cuboid shaped solids, the area of opposite surfaces is same. Area of face (i) = length × breadth = ℓ × b. Area of face (ii) = breadth × height = b × h. Area of face (iii) = height × length = h × ℓ. So, the total surface area of cuboid = 2 × {Area of face (i) + Area of face (ii) + Area of face (iii)}:

Surface area of cuboid: S = 2{(ℓ × b) + (b × h) + (h × ℓ)}

Example 18 — The figure shows a rectangular cuboid 9 cm long, 8 cm wide and 7 cm high. Find the total surface area of cuboid.

Step 1: Length of cuboid = ℓ = 9 cm, breadth of cuboid = b = 8 cm, height of cuboid = h = 7 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Surface area of cuboid = 2{(ℓ × b) + (b × h) + (h × ℓ)}

Step 3: Substitute: = 2{(9 × 8) + (8 × 7) + (7 × 9)} = 2{72 + 56 + 63} = 2{191} = 382 cm².

Final answer: The total surface area of cuboid is 382 cm².

Volume of cube

As we are familiar that the length, breadth and height are same in any cube: length = breadth = height. So we can use the formula to find volume of cube:

Volume of cube = length × length × length, i.e. V = ℓ × ℓ × ℓ = ℓ³

Worked example — Practice-9

Find the volume of cube having length of each side 7 cm.

Step 1: ℓ = 7 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Volume of cube = V = ℓ³

Step 3: V = 7 × 7 × 7 = 343 cm³.

Final answer: 343 cm³

Example 19 — A room is shaped like a cube. Its measurement is 9 m on each edge. What is the total volume and total surface area of 5 such rooms?

Step 1: Length of an edge of a room = ℓ = 9 m.

Step 2: Write the formula: Surface area of cube = 6 × (length)² = 6ℓ²

Step 3: Surface area of one room = 6(9)² = 6 × 81 = 486 m². Surface area of 5 rooms = 5 × 486 = 2430 m².

Step 4: Write the formula: Volume of cube = (length)³, i.e. V = ℓ³

Step 5: Volume of one room = (9)³ = 729 m³. Volume of 5 rooms = 5 × 729 = 3645 m³.

Final answer: The surface area of 5 rooms is 2430 m² and the volume of 5 rooms is 3645 m³.

Volume of cuboid

In the cuboid shape solids the measurement of atleast one edge is different from other two edges. So, we can use the formula to find volume of cuboid:

Volume of cuboid = length × breadth × height, i.e. V = ℓ × b × h

Example 20 — Find the volume of cuboid if it is 7 cm long, 5 cm wide and 5 cm high

Step 1: Length of cuboid = ℓ = 7 cm, breadth of cuboid = b = 5 cm, height of cuboid = h = 5 cm.

Step 2: Write the formula: Volume of cuboid = length × breadth × height (V = ℓ × b × h)

Step 3: V = 7 × 5 × 5 = 175 cm³.

Final answer: The volume of the cuboid is 175 cm³.

Worked example — Practice-9 (container)

A container is 20 m long, 3 m wide and 5 m high. What is the surface area and volume of the container?

Step 1: ℓ = 20 m, b = 3 m, h = 5 m.

Step 2: Write the formula: Surface area of cuboid = 2{(ℓ × b) + (b × h) + (h × ℓ)}

Step 3: Surface area = 2{(20 × 3) + (3 × 5) + (5 × 20)} = 2{60 + 15 + 100} = 2{175} = 350 m².

Step 4: Write the formula: Volume of cuboid = ℓ × b × h = 20 × 3 × 5 = 300 m³.

Final answer: Surface area = 350 m², Volume = 300 m³

Example 21 — Find the total surface area of a solid cuboid of volume 560 cm³ with 10 cm of length and 7 cm of breadth

Step 1: Volume of solid cuboid = V = 560 cm³, length = ℓ = 10 cm, breadth = b = 7 cm.

Step 2: Write the relation: Height of solid cuboid = Volume of solid cuboid / (length × breadth), i.e. h = V/(ℓ × b).

Step 3: h = 560/(10 × 7) = 560/70 = 8 cm.

Step 4: Write the formula: Total surface area of solid cuboid = 2{(length × breadth) + (breadth × height) + (height × length)}

Step 5: Substitute: = 2{(10 × 7) + (7 × 8) + (8 × 10)} = 2{70 + 56 + 80} = 2 × 206 = 412 cm².

Final answer: The total surface area of solid cuboid is 412 cm².

Worked examples — Exercise 8.3, Question 1: Find the volume and surface area of the following figures

(i) Cuboid of length 5 cm, breadth 4 cm and height 3 cm

Step 1: ℓ = 5 cm, b = 4 cm, h = 3 cm.

Step 2: Write the formulae: Volume of cuboid = ℓ × b × h and Surface area of cuboid = 2{(ℓ × b) + (b × h) + (h × ℓ)}.

Step 3: Volume = 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 cm³.

Step 4: Surface area = 2{(5 × 4) + (4 × 3) + (3 × 5)} = 2{20 + 12 + 15} = 2{47} = 94 cm².

Final answer: Volume = 60 cm³, Surface area = 94 cm² (Note: the book's Answers key prints 96 cm² for this part; the working above follows the printed dimensions.)

(ii) Cube of side 9 cm

Step 1: ℓ = 9 cm.

Step 2: Write the formulae: Volume of cube = ℓ³ and Surface area of cube = 6ℓ².

Step 3: Volume = 9 × 9 × 9 = 729 cm³.

Step 4: Surface area = 6(9)² = 6 × 81 = 486 cm².

Final answer: Volume = 729 cm³, Surface area = 486 cm²

(iii) Cuboid of length 49 mm, breadth 30 mm and height 35 mm

Step 1: ℓ = 49 mm, b = 30 mm, h = 35 mm.

Step 2: Write the formulae: Volume of cuboid = ℓ × b × h and Surface area of cuboid = 2{(ℓ × b) + (b × h) + (h × ℓ)}.

Step 3: Volume = 49 × 30 × 35 = 51,450 mm³.

Step 4: Surface area = 2{(49 × 30) + (30 × 35) + (35 × 49)} = 2{1470 + 1050 + 1715} = 2{4235} = 8470 mm².

Final answer: Volume = 51,450 mm³, Surface area = 8470 mm²

Worked examples — Exercise 8.3, Question 2: Complete the table for each solid shape

Formulae used in every row: Surface area of cuboid = 2{(ℓ × b) + (b × h) + (h × ℓ)} and Volume of cuboid = ℓ × b × h.

(i) Length 7 cm, Breadth 8 cm, Height 8 cm

Step 1: Surface area = 2{(7 × 8) + (8 × 8) + (8 × 7)} = 2{56 + 64 + 56} = 2{176} = 352 cm².

Step 2: Volume = 7 × 8 × 8 = 448 cm³.

Final answer: Surface area = 352 cm², Volume = 448 cm³

(ii) Breadth 10 cm, Height 10 cm, Volume 950 cm³ — find Length and Surface area

Step 1: Length = Volume / (breadth × height) = 950/(10 × 10) = 950/100 = 9.5 cm.

Step 2: Surface area = 2{(9.5 × 10) + (10 × 10) + (10 × 9.5)} = 2{95 + 100 + 95} = 2{290} = 580 cm².

Final answer: Length = 9.5 cm, Surface area = 580 cm²

(iii) Length 18 cm, Height 20 cm, Volume 1080 cm³ — find Breadth and Surface area

Step 1: Breadth = Volume / (length × height) = 1080/(18 × 20) = 1080/360 = 3 cm.

Step 2: Surface area = 2{(18 × 3) + (3 × 20) + (20 × 18)} = 2{54 + 60 + 360} = 2{474} = 948 cm².

Final answer: Breadth = 3 cm, Surface area = 948 cm²

(iv) Length 7 cm, Breadth 16 cm, Surface area 200 cm² — find Height and Volume

Step 1: Using the formula, Surface area = 2{(7 × 16) + (16 × h) + (h × 7)} = 2{112 + 23h}.

Step 2: Even with height almost zero, 2 × 112 = 224 cm², which is already more than the printed surface area of 200 cm². So no positive height satisfies this row.

Final answer: This row cannot be completed: the printed data (length 7 cm, breadth 16 cm, surface area 200 cm²) is inconsistent, because the two length × breadth faces alone have area 2 × 7 × 16 = 224 cm². (The book's Answers key prints height 0.5 cm and volume 56 cm³ for this row, which also do not satisfy the printed surface area.)

(v) Length 15 cm, Height 15 cm, Volume 2025 cm³ — find Breadth and Surface area

Step 1: Breadth = Volume / (length × height) = 2025/(15 × 15) = 2025/225 = 9 cm.

Step 2: Surface area = 2{(15 × 9) + (9 × 15) + (15 × 15)} = 2{135 + 135 + 225} = 2{495} = 990 cm².

Final answer: Breadth = 9 cm, Surface area = 990 cm²

(vi) Breadth 17 m, Height 17 m, Surface area 1734 m² — find Length and Volume

Step 1: 1734 = 2{(ℓ × 17) + (17 × 17) + (17 × ℓ)} = 2{34ℓ + 289}. So 867 = 34ℓ + 289, giving 34ℓ = 578 and ℓ = 17 m.

Step 2: Volume = 17 × 17 × 17 = 4913 m³.

Final answer: Length = 17 m, Volume = 4913 m³

(vii) Length 11 mm, Height 11 mm, Volume 1331 mm³ — find Breadth and Surface area

Step 1: Breadth = Volume / (length × height) = 1331/(11 × 11) = 1331/121 = 11 mm.

Step 2: All three dimensions are 11 mm, so it is a cube: Surface area = 6ℓ² = 6 × 121 = 726 mm².

Final answer: Breadth = 11 mm, Surface area = 726 mm²

(ii)9.5 cm10 cm10 cm580 cm²950 cm³
