Worked examples — Exercise 8.3, Questions 3 to 9

Q3. A container is 50 m long, 20 m wide and 25 m high. Find the capacity of the container.

Step 1: Capacity means volume. Write the formula: Volume of cuboid = ℓ × b × h

Step 2: Volume = 50 × 20 × 25 = 25,000 m³.

Final answer: The capacity of the container is 25,000 m³.

Q4. The inside of a cubical box measures 15 cm on each edge. How many cubes each measuring 1 cm on each edge will fit inside the box?

Step 1: Write the formula: Volume of cube = ℓ³. Volume of the box = 15 × 15 × 15 = 3375 cm³.

Step 2: Volume of one small cube = 1 × 1 × 1 = 1 cm³.

Step 3: Number of cubes = 3375/1 = 3375.

Final answer: 3375 cubes will fit inside the box.

Q5. Find the total surface area of a solid cube of volume 8000 cm³.

Step 1: Write the formula: Volume of cube = ℓ³. So ℓ³ = 8000, giving ℓ = 20 cm (because 20 × 20 × 20 = 8000).

Step 2: Write the formula: Surface area of cube = 6ℓ² = 6 × (20)² = 6 × 400 = 2400 cm².

Final answer: Total surface area = 2400 cm²

Q6. How much water can a cubical water tank contain if it is 6 m long, 3 m wide and 5 m high?

Step 1: The amount of water is the volume of the tank. Write the formula: Volume = length × breadth × height (V = ℓ × b × h)

Step 2: Volume = 6 × 3 × 5 = 90 m³.

Final answer: The tank can contain 90 m³ of water.

Q7. A wall has to be built with length 19 m, thickness 3.5 m and height 9 m. What is the volume of the wall in cubic metres?

Step 1: The wall is a cuboid; its thickness is its breadth. Write the formula: Volume of cuboid = ℓ × b × h

Step 2: Volume = 19 × 3.5 × 9 = 598.5 m³.

Final answer: The volume of the wall is 598.5 m³.

Q8. Hamza wants to wrap a gift pack in a box for his brother. The top and bottom of the box are 32 cm by 15 cm. The sides are 9 cm by 8 cm, and the front and back are also 9 cm by 8 cm. How much wrapping paper will be used to wrap the gift pack?

Step 1: Wrapping paper needed = total surface area = sum of the areas of all six faces.

Step 2: Top + bottom = 2 × (32 × 15) = 2 × 480 = 960 cm².

Step 3: Two sides = 2 × (9 × 8) = 2 × 72 = 144 cm².

Step 4: Front + back = 2 × (9 × 8) = 2 × 72 = 144 cm².

Step 5: Total = 960 + 144 + 144 = 1248 cm².

Final answer: 1248 cm² of wrapping paper will be used.

Q9. A metal cupboard is 3 m long, 400 cm high and 1000 mm wide. What is the cost of painting the cupboard at the rate of Rs. 100 per m²?

Step 1: First convert all dimensions into the same unit (metres): length = 3 m; height = 400 cm = 400/100 = 4 m; width (breadth) = 1000 mm = 1000/1000 = 1 m.

Step 2: Write the formula: Surface area of cuboid = 2{(ℓ × b) + (b × h) + (h × ℓ)}

Step 3: Surface area = 2{(3 × 1) + (1 × 4) + (4 × 3)} = 2{3 + 4 + 12} = 2{19} = 38 m².

Step 4: Cost of painting = 38 × 100 = Rs. 3800.

Final answer: The cost of painting the cupboard is Rs. 3800.

Summary

  • The distance around any two dimensional closed shape is called perimeter.
  • The region enclosed within the boundary of a closed shape is called area.
  • Perimeter of square = 4 × side length = 4ℓ; Area of square = side length × side length = ℓ × ℓ = ℓ².
  • Perimeter of rectangle = 2(length + breadth) = 2(ℓ + b); Area of rectangle = length × breadth = (ℓ × b).
  • Area of path = Area of larger shape − Area of smaller shape.
  • The altitude is also known as perpendicular height.
  • A parallelogram is a 4-sided closed shape formed by two pairs of parallel lines. Area of parallelogram = base length × perpendicular height.
  • A trapezium is a quadrilateral with four sides and four angles. It has only two parallel sides. Area of trapezium = (1/2)(S₁ + S₂) × h.
  • Area of triangle = (1/2)(b × h).
  • The volume is a quantity or amount of space enclosed by a closed surface or container.
  • The surface area of a solid figure is the sum of the area of all its faces.
  • 3-dimensional figures/shapes are the solid figures which have thickness and can be held in human hand.
  • A 3-dimensional solid body bounded by six square surfaces is known as cube.
  • A 3-dimensional solid body bounded by six rectangular surfaces is known as cuboid.
  • Surface area of cuboid: S = 2[(ℓ × b) + (b × h) + (h × ℓ)]; Surface area of cube: S = 6ℓ².
  • Volume of cuboid: V = ℓ × b × h; Volume of cube: V = ℓ³.

mcqs.q: In a cube, how are the length, breadth and height related?
options: Breadth is different from both length and height
mcqs.why: The notes state that in a cube the length, breadth and height are the same: length = breadth = height.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the surface area of a cube of side l?
mcqs.why: A cube has 6 equal faces, each of area l x l, so the notes give: Surface area of cube = 6 x (length)^2 = 6l^2.

mcqs.q: Find the total surface area of a cube with each side 8 cm long.
mcqs.why: Formula: Surface area of cube = 6l^2. Working: 6 x (8)^2 = 6 x 64 = 384 cm^2.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the total surface area of a cuboid with length l, breadth b and height h?
options: S = 2{(l x b) + (b x h) + (h x l)}
S = (l x b) + (b x h) + (h x l)
S = 6{(l x b) + (b x h) + (h x l)}
S = l x b x h
mcqs.why: Opposite faces of a cuboid are equal, with face areas l x b, b x h and h x l, so the notes give S = 2{(l x b) + (b x h) + (h x l)}.

mcqs.q: Find the total surface area of a cuboid 9 cm long, 8 cm wide and 7 cm high.
Find the volume of a cube having length of each side 7 cm.
mcqs.why: Formula: Volume of cube V = l^3 = l x l x l. Working: V = 7 x 7 x 7 = 343 cm^3.

mcqs.q: Find the volume of a cuboid 7 cm long, 5 cm wide and 5 cm high.
mcqs.why: Formula: Volume of cuboid V = l x b x h. Working: V = 7 x 5 x 5 = 175 cm^3.

mcqs.q: A room is shaped like a cube with 9 m on each edge. What is the total volume of 5 such rooms?
mcqs.why: Formula: Volume of cube V = l^3. Working: one room = 9^3 = 729 m^3, so 5 rooms = 5 x 729 = 3645 m^3.

mcqs.q: A solid cuboid has volume 560 cm^3, length 10 cm and breadth 7 cm. What is its total surface area?
Find the surface area of a cuboid of length 5 cm, breadth 4 cm and height 3 cm.
mcqs.why: Formula: S = 2{(l x b) + (b x h) + (h x l)}. Working: 2{(5x4)+(4x3)+(3x5)} = 2{20+12+15} = 2x47 = 94 cm^2. The book key prints 96 cm^2, which does not match these dimensions.

lessons.title: 9.1 Identification of 2-D and 3-D Shapes with Respect to Their Characteristics
lessons.notes_html:
1-Dimensional, 2-Dimensional and 3-Dimensional Figures

We are familiar with different types of geometrical shapes such as line, rays, triangles, rectangles and other types like polygons. Some of them are one-dimensional figures and some are two-dimensional figures.

1-Dimensional figures: The figures that have only length are called 1-D figures. These figures do not have width or thickness. For example, the book shows a line segment, a ray, a curve line and a line.

2-Dimensional figures: The figures that can be drawn on paper are called 2-D figures. These figures have no thickness but they have width and height. For example, the book shows a square (with width and height marked), a rectangle and a triangle.

3-Dimensional figures: The solid figures are 3-dimensional figures. These figures have height, width and depth. All solid figures have thickness and can be held in our hand.

i. Cube

A 3-dimensional solid body bounded by six square surfaces is known as a cube. The book shows a cube labelled A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H and its net (a cross-shaped net of six squares).

  • Square surfaces: (i) ABCD and EFGH (opposite surfaces), (ii) ABFE and DCGH (opposite surfaces), (iii) ADHE and BCGF (opposite surfaces).
  • Vertices: There are 8 vertices of a cube, i.e. A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H.
  • Edges: There are 12 edges of a cube, i.e. AB, BC, CD, AD, BF, FG, GC, GH, HE, HD, AE and EF.

ii. Cuboid

A 3-dimensional solid body bounded by six rectangular surfaces is known as a cuboid. The book shows a cuboid and its net.

  • Rectangular surfaces: (i) ABCD and EFGH (opposite surfaces), (ii) ADHE and BCGF (opposite surfaces), (iii) ABFE and DCGH (opposite surfaces).
  • Vertices: There are 8 vertices of a cuboid, i.e. A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H.
  • Edges: There are 12 edges of a cuboid, i.e. AB, BC, CD, AD, BF, FG, GC, GH, HE, HD, AE and EF.

iii. Cylinder

A 3-dimensional solid body with two circular surfaces of equal radius and one curved surface between them is known as a cylinder. The book shows a cylinder and its net (a rectangle with a circle at each end).

  • Surfaces: A cylinder has 2 circular and 1 curved surface (3 surfaces in all).
  • Vertices: A cylinder has no vertex.
  • Edges: It has 2 edges.

iv. Sphere

A 3-dimensional solid body with a completely round surface whose all points on its outer surface are at an equal distance from a fixed point is known as a sphere. In the book's figure, the fixed point is called the centre (F) and the distance from the centre to a point P on the surface is called the radius of the sphere.

iv. Hemisphere

A 3-D shape made from cutting a sphere into two equal halves with one flat side is known as a hemisphere.

  • Surfaces: It has one flat and one curved surface.
  • Vertices: It has no vertex.
  • Edges: It has one curved edge.

v. Cone

A 3-dimensional solid body with one circular surface and a slanting curved surface is known as a cone. The book shows a cone and its net (a circle with a sector).

  • Surfaces: A cone has two surfaces.
  • Vertices: A cone has only one vertex.
  • Edges: A cone has only one edge.

Note from the book: The distance between the centre of the base of a cone and its vertex is called the height of the cone. The distance of the vertex from any point on the boundary is known as its slant height.

Worked Examples — Exercise 9.1

Q1. Write the name of the 3-dimensional figures which resemble these objects (answers as given in the book's Answers section):

  • (i) Mobile phones — Cuboid, because the object is a solid with rectangular surfaces.
  • (ii) Birthday cap — Cone, because it has a circular base and a slanting curved surface meeting at one vertex.
  • (iii) Football — Sphere, because it is completely round.
  • (iv) Dice — Cube, because it is bounded by six square surfaces.
  • (v) Water tank (drum) — Cylinder, because it has two circular surfaces and one curved surface.
  • (vi) Bowl — Hemisphere, because it is half of a sphere with one flat side.

Q2. Sort 1-D, 2-D and 3-D shapes:

  • 1-D: (iv) Line — it has only length.
  • 2-D: (ii) Rectangle, (v) Square, (vii) Triangle — they can be drawn on paper and have width and height but no thickness.
  • 3-D: (i) Cone, (iii) Cylinder, (vi) Cube, (viii) Cuboid — they are solid figures with height, width and depth.

Q3. Edges, surfaces and vertices (from the characteristics given in this lesson):

  • (i) Cylinder: Surfaces = 3, Vertices = 0, Edges = 2.
  • (ii) Cuboid: Surfaces = 6, Vertices = 8, Edges = 12.
  • (iii) Cube: Surfaces = 6, Vertices = 8, Edges = 12.
  • (iv) Cone: Surfaces = 2 (one circular surface and one slanting curved surface), Vertices = 1, Edges = 1.
  • (v) Hemisphere: Surfaces = 2 (one flat and one curved surface), Vertices = 0, Edges = 1 (curved edge).

mcqs.q: Which of these is a 1-dimensional figure?
mcqs.why: A line has only length and no width or thickness, so the notes classify a line as a 1-dimensional figure.

mcqs.q: What do 2-dimensional figures have?
options: Width and height but no thickness
Thickness, so they can be held in the hand
mcqs.why: The notes say 2-D figures can be drawn on paper and have width and height, but they have no thickness at all.

mcqs.q: How many vertices and edges does a cube have?
mcqs.why: The notes list the cube's vertices as A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H, which are 8 in total, and list 12 edges for the cube.

mcqs.q: A cuboid is bounded by six surfaces of which shape?
mcqs.why: The notes define a cuboid as a 3-dimensional solid body bounded by six rectangular surfaces, unlike a cube which has square surfaces.

mcqs.q: How many surfaces does a cylinder have in all?
mcqs.why: Working: a cylinder has 2 circular surfaces plus 1 curved surface, so 2 + 1 = 3 surfaces in all, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: In a sphere, all points on its outer surface are at an equal distance from which point?
mcqs.why: The notes define a sphere by this property: every point on its surface is at an equal distance from a fixed point called the centre.

mcqs.q: What surfaces does a hemisphere have?
options: One flat surface and one curved surface
Two circular surfaces and one curved surface
One circular surface and one slanting surface
mcqs.why: A hemisphere is half of a sphere cut into two equal halves, so the notes give it one flat surface and one curved surface.

mcqs.q: How many vertices and edges does a cone have?
options: Only one vertex and only one edge
mcqs.why: The notes state clearly that a cone has only one vertex, where its slanting curved surface meets, and only one edge.

mcqs.q: Which 3-dimensional figure does a dice resemble?
mcqs.why: The worked example says a dice is a cube because it is bounded by six square surfaces, matching the definition of a cube in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is the height of a cone?
options: The distance from its vertex to any point on the boundary
The distance around its circular base
The distance between the centre of its base and its vertex
The distance across its circular base
mcqs.why: The notes define the height of a cone as the distance between the centre of the base and its vertex; the vertex-to-boundary distance is the slant height.

lessons.title: 9.2 Parallel Lines, Intersecting Lines, Perpendicular Lines and Transversal
lessons.notes_html:
Remember — Line, Ray and Line Segment

  • Line: A line is a series of points that extends in both directions without ends, e.g. line AB.
  • Ray: A ray is a line with one end point, e.g. ray AB starting at A.
  • Line segment: A line segment is a part of a line that is made by joining two points together, e.g. segment AB.

i. Parallel Lines

The railway track and zebra crossing never intersect each other at any point. “Two or more lines which extend in the same direction and remain the same distance apart are called parallel lines.” In the book's figures, the parallel lines are represented by the single or double arrow marks drawn on them. The symbol ∥ is used to represent the parallel lines.

ii. Intersecting Lines / Non-Parallel Lines

The legs of the table and the hands of a scissors are crossing each other. “Two lines that are intersecting each other at a single point are called intersecting lines.” The point where these lines intersect is called the point of intersection. In the book's figure (a), two lines cross at point P, and in figure (b) many lines pass through one point O.

iii. Perpendicular Lines

Examples from our surroundings given in the book: a tall tree on the ground; an electric pole or the pole of our national flag on the pavement; the corner of two adjacent walls and high buildings. “Two or more lines that meet or intersect each other at right angle (90°) are called perpendicular lines.” The book shows two pairs of perpendicular lines, each marked with a small square at the point of intersection to show the right angle.

Fun Fact (book): Perpendicular lines are always intersecting lines, but intersecting lines may or may not be perpendicular.

iv. Transversal

“A line that passes through two or more lines at two distinct points is called transversal.” In Figure 9.2.1 of the book, a line PQ passes through the pair of parallel lines AB and CD. The line PQ is called the transversal. The transversal makes eight angles: a, b, c, d at line AB and e, f, g, h at line CD.

Transversal Angles

When a transversal intersects two parallel or non-parallel lines, it forms different kinds of angles. From Figure 9.2.1, the book gives this table:

Sr. No.Type of anglesAngles
1Interior angles∠c, ∠d, ∠e, ∠f
2Exterior angles∠a, ∠b, ∠g, ∠h
3Pairs of corresponding angles∠a and ∠e, ∠b and ∠f, ∠c and ∠g, ∠d and ∠h
4Pairs of alternate interior angles∠c and ∠f, ∠d and ∠e
5Pairs of alternate exterior angles∠a and ∠h, ∠b and ∠g
6Pairs of interior angles on the same side of transversal∠c and ∠e, ∠d and ∠f

From the above discussion, the book concludes that the angles associated with the transversal have the following properties:

  • (i) The corresponding angles are equal in measurement.
  • (ii) The alternate angles are equal in measurement.
  • (iii) The interior angles are supplementary.

The converse statements are also true:

  • (i) If the corresponding angles are equal, then the two lines are parallel.
  • (ii) If the alternate angles are equal, the two lines are parallel.
  • (iii) If the interior angles are supplementary, then the two lines are parallel.

Vertically Opposite Angles

“When two lines intersect at a point, then the opposite angles are formed at the point of intersection. These angles are called vertically opposite angles.” In Figure 9.2.2 of the book, ∠a and ∠d, and ∠b and ∠c are vertically opposite angles. Remember: A pair of vertically opposite angles are always equal to each other.

Example 1 (Book)

If the measure of angle a = 60°, find the values of the other angles on the intersecting lines AB and CD (Figure 9.2.3).

Solution: As vertically opposite angles are equal, so m∠a = m∠d = 60°. Since ∠a and ∠b are supplementary, m∠a + m∠b = 180°, so 60° + m∠b = 180°, m∠b = 180° − 60° = 120°. Now, by applying the property of vertically opposite angles, m∠b = m∠c = 120°.

Example 2 (Book)

Calculate the values of the unknown angles in Figure 9.2.4, where AB and CD are parallel lines and T₁ and T₂ are the transversals. One angle on T₁ is 107° and one angle on T₂ is 70°.

Solution — For transversal T₁: m∠j = 107° (vertically opposite angles). m∠i + 107° = 180° (adjacent angles on a line are supplementary), so m∠i = 180° − 107° = 73°. m∠i = m∠h = 73° (vertically opposite angles). Now m∠i = m∠n = 73° (alternate angles are equal) and m∠k = 107°. Also m∠k = m∠l = 107° and m∠n = m∠m = 73° (vertically opposite angles are equal).

Solution — For transversal T₂: m∠a = 70° (vertically opposite angles are equal). m∠a + m∠b = 180° (adjacent angles on a line are supplementary), so 70° + m∠b = 180°, m∠b = 180° − 70° = 110°. So m∠b = m∠c = 110° (vertically opposite angles are equal). Now m∠b = m∠d = 110° (corresponding angles are equal), m∠d = m∠e = 110° (vertically opposite angles), and m∠a = m∠g = 70° and m∠f = 70° (m∠f = m∠g).

Practice Answers (Book Practice-2, Practice-3 and Practice-4)

  • Practice-2: (i) Lines PQ and RS, drawn with the same arrow marks and never meeting, are parallel lines. (ii) Lines AD and CB cross each other at a single point, so they are intersecting lines.
  • Practice-3: Only figure (ii), where lines PQ and SR meet at a right angle, shows perpendicular lines. Figures (i) and (iii) show lines that are not perpendicular.
  • Practice-4: In the figure, two parallel lines are cut by a transversal and one angle is 160°. The angle x and the 160° angle are interior angles on the same side situation giving supplementary angles, so x + 160° = 180° and x = 20°.

Worked Examples — Exercise 9.2

Q1. Identify the parallel, intersecting and perpendicular lines (answers as given in the book's Answers section):

  • (i) Parallel lines — the two lines carry the same arrow marks, go in the same direction and stay the same distance apart.
  • (ii) Intersecting lines — the two lines cross each other at a single point.
  • (iii) Intersecting lines — the two lines cross each other at a single point.
  • (iv) Parallel lines — the two lines go in the same direction and never meet.
  • (v) Intersecting lines — the two lines cross each other at a single point.
  • (vi) Intersecting lines — the two lines are not parallel; they meet at a point.

Q2. Find the unknown angles of the intersecting lines:

  • (i) The given angle is 30°. Angle a is vertically opposite to 30°, so a = 30°. Angles b and c are supplementary to 30° and vertically opposite to each other, so b = 150° and c = 150°.
  • (ii) The given angle is 120°. Angle r is vertically opposite to 120°, so r = 120°. Angles p and q are supplementary to 120° and vertically opposite to each other, so p = 60° and q = 60°.

Q3. Observe the diagram (two transversals T₁ and T₂ cutting two lines, with angles a to p) and write all:

  • (i) Pairs of corresponding angles: d and f, b and h, a and g, c and e, m and i, l and o, n and j, k and p.
  • (ii) Pairs of alternate angles: d and e, a and h, m and k, n and l.
  • (iii) Exterior angles: f and b, c and g, i and o, j and p (the angles lying outside the two lines).

Q4. Calculate the values of the unknown angles in the following diagrams (answers as given in the book's Answers section):

  • (i) x is supplementary to the given arrangement of the 100° angle on the parallel lines cut by transversal T₁, giving x = 80°.
  • (ii) Lines NO and LM are parallel and cut by transversal T₁; the 60° angle and x are supplementary, so x = 180° − 60° = 120°.
  • (iii) The angle 3x is supplementary to 111°, so 3x = 180° − 111° = 69°, and x = 23.
  • (iv) The interior angles 6x and 2x on the same side of transversal T₁ are supplementary, so 6x + 2x = 180°, 8x = 180°, and x = 22.5.
  • (v) At the point where the two transversals meet the middle line, the angles next to x on the straight line are 180° − 110° = 70° and 180° − 150° = 30°, so x = 180° − 70° − 30° = 80°.

mcqs.q: What is a ray?
options: A part of a line joining two points
A line with one end point
A line extending in both directions without ends
mcqs.why: The notes define a ray as a line with one end point, for example ray AB starting at A, unlike a line which has no ends.

mcqs.q: Which statement about parallel lines is correct?
options: They intersect at a single point
They meet at a right angle of 90 degrees
They extend in the same direction and remain the same distance apart
They pass through two lines at distinct points
mcqs.why: The notes define parallel lines as lines extending in the same direction and remaining the same distance apart, so they never intersect.

mcqs.q: What is the point called where two intersecting lines cross each other?
mcqs.why: The notes say two lines intersecting at a single point are intersecting lines, and that single crossing point is called the point of intersection.

mcqs.q: Perpendicular lines meet or intersect each other at which angle?
mcqs.why: The notes define perpendicular lines as lines that meet or intersect at a right angle, which is 90 degrees, marked by a small square.

mcqs.q: Which statement is true according to the book's Fun Fact?
options: Perpendicular lines are always intersecting lines
mcqs.why: The Fun Fact states perpendicular lines are always intersecting lines, but intersecting lines may or may not be perpendicular to each other.

mcqs.q: What is a transversal?
options: A line that joins two points only
A line with one end point
A line that passes through two or more lines at two distinct points
A pair of lines the same distance apart
mcqs.why: The notes define a transversal as a line passing through two or more lines at two distinct points, like line PQ cutting lines AB and CD.

mcqs.q: In Figure 9.2.1, which angles are the interior angles formed by the transversal?
options: Angles c, d, e and f
Angles a, b, g and h
Angles a, e, b and f only
Angles c, g, d and h only
mcqs.why: The table in the notes lists the interior angles as c, d, e and f, while a, b, g and h are listed as the exterior angles.

mcqs.q: Which is a pair of alternate interior angles in Figure 9.2.1?
mcqs.why: The notes' table gives the pairs of alternate interior angles as c and f, and d and e, so angle c with angle f is one such pair.

mcqs.q: Two intersecting lines have one angle a = 60 degrees. What is the angle vertically opposite to a, and what is the adjacent angle b?
mcqs.why: Working: vertically opposite angles are equal, so the opposite angle is 60 degrees. Adjacent angles are supplementary: b = 180 - 60 = 120 degrees.

mcqs.q: An angle x and a 160 degree angle are interior angles on the same side of a transversal cutting parallel lines. What is x?
mcqs.why: Working: interior angles on the same side are supplementary, so x + 160 = 180, giving x = 180 - 160 = 20 degrees, as in Practice-4.

lessons.title: 9.3 Symmetry
lessons.notes_html:
What is Symmetry?

Symmetry is all around us in nature and in the field of art and design. The book shows leaves, a butterfly and a flower, and asks how we can identify the symmetrical lines in them. Symmetry is defined as: “One shape is identical to the other shape when it is moved, rotated or flipped; then we say this shape is in symmetrical shape.”

“A line that divides an object into two identical pieces is called line of symmetry.”

9.3.1 Types of Symmetry

The book discusses two types of symmetry: (i) Reflective symmetry, (ii) Rotational symmetry.

i. Reflective Symmetry

“If a shape or pattern is reflected in a mirror line or line of symmetry, then this type of symmetry is called reflective symmetry.” For example, the book shows (a) the reflection of a mountain in the lake, where the mirror line divides the figure into two parts, and (b) a butterfly, where the left side is the reflection of the right side across the dashed line of symmetry. In the above figures, the mirror line divides the figures into two parts.

Example 3 (Book) — Completing Shapes on a Mirror Line

Complete the shapes (i) a rectangle, (ii) a U-notched shape and (iii) a semicircle, drawn on grids above a given mirror line. Solution (book): Draw the same shape on the other side of the mirror line or line of symmetry. Simply, flip the shapes and complete them. In the book's solution figures: (i) the rectangle is completed below the line to make a larger rectangle; (ii) the notched shape is flipped below the line to complete the figure; (iii) the semicircle is completed above the line to make a full circle.

Practice-5 (book): Look at the pattern in the grid. If the pattern is reflected in the two lines of symmetry, find what colour the labelled squares A to I will be: copy the pattern and colour the rest of the corresponding squares when it is reflected in the mirror lines. The rule is the same as Example 3: every coloured square is flipped across each mirror line to the square in the matching position.

ii. Rotational Symmetry

Observe in your surroundings: some of the shapes you see will have a line of symmetry, but some of the shapes look the same as you turn them, e.g. the book shows (a) a pedestal fan, (b) the wheels of a tractor and (c) a circular table. “If a shape rotated about a point to another position and still looks the same, then the shape has rotational symmetry.” In the above figures, all the shapes have rotational symmetry.

“Number of times a shape looks the same in one full turn is called order of symmetry.” For example, the book shows a rectangle and the letter “S”: this rectangle and the letter “S” have rotational symmetry of order 2.

Remember (book): A fixed point around which the rotation occurs is called the centre of rotation.

Example 4 (Book) — Order of Symmetry of a Square

Rotate the square (divided into four small squares with the top-right small square shaded, centre O) and find the order of symmetry. Solution: The book shows the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th rotations, in which the shaded small square moves to the bottom-right, bottom-left and top-left positions and then back. At the 4th rotation the figure came to its original position. So, the order of symmetry is 4 around 90°.

Practice-6 (book): Draw a circle, a rectangle, a rhombus and a kite, rotate each figure at 90°, and write the order of symmetry for each shape, using the counting method of Example 4. For the rectangle, the book has already told us the order is 2.

Worked Examples — Exercise 9.3

Q1. Use the concept of reflective symmetry to complete the following shapes. Method (from Example 3): flip the given part across the dotted mirror line and draw the same part on the other side, square by square on the grid.

  • (i) The blue triangle below the horizontal mirror line is flipped above the line, completing a symmetric diamond-like figure.
  • (ii) The blue semicircle on the left of the vertical mirror line is flipped to the right, completing a full circle.
  • (iii) The blue shape on the right of the vertical mirror line is flipped to the left, completing the symmetric shape.
  • (iv) The two small blue triangles are flipped across the diagonal mirror line to complete the figure on the other side of the line.
  • (v) The blue shape is flipped across the vertical mirror line to complete the figure.
  • (vi) The blue F-like shape on the left of the vertical mirror line is flipped to the right, completing the symmetric figure.

Q2. Rotate the following shapes and write the order of symmetry:

  • (i) The flower-like figure inside a circle with centre O has three identical petals, so it looks the same 3 times in one full turn: order 3.
  • (ii) The circle with centre O divided into four quarters follows the same counting as Example 4: at the 4th rotation it comes to its original position, so the order of symmetry is 4.
  • (iii) The triangle drawn at point O does not look the same again until one full turn is completed, so its order of symmetry is 1.

Q3. Draw the possible lines of symmetry for the following shapes:

  • (i) Leaf: 1 line of symmetry, along the middle of the leaf.
  • (ii) Parallelogram (as drawn): no line of symmetry — no mirror line divides it into two identical pieces.
  • (iii) Trapezium (with two equal slanting sides, as drawn): 1 line of symmetry, the vertical line through its centre.
  • (iv) Letter T: 1 line of symmetry, the vertical line through its centre.
  • (v) Letter P: no line of symmetry.
  • (vi) Letter U: 1 line of symmetry, the vertical line through its centre.
  • Q4. A shape with exactly two lines of symmetry: a rectangle — the vertical line and the horizontal line through its centre are its two lines of symmetry.
  • Q5. A shape with exactly 6 lines of symmetry: a regular hexagon — it has 6 lines of symmetry.
  • Q6. A shape with exactly 3 order of rotation: a shape with three identical parts around its centre, like the three-petal figure of Q2(i), has order of rotation 3.
  • Q7. A shape with exactly 6 order of rotation: a regular hexagon (or a flower with six identical petals) has order of rotation 6.

Q8. Find the order of rotational symmetry for the following shapes:

  • (i) Square: order 4 (as found in Example 4).
  • (ii) Five-pointed star: order 5 — it looks the same 5 times in one full turn.
  • (iii) L-shape: order 1 — it looks the same only after one full turn.

mcqs.q: What is a line of symmetry?
options: A line that divides an object into two identical pieces
A line joining the centre to the surface
A line that passes through two other lines
A line around which a shape is rotated
mcqs.why: The notes define a line of symmetry exactly as a line that divides an object into two identical pieces, like the dashed line in a butterfly.

mcqs.q: The reflection of a mountain in a lake is an example of which type of symmetry?
mcqs.why: The notes give the mountain reflected in the lake as an example of reflective symmetry, where the mirror line divides the figure into two parts.

mcqs.q: A semicircle drawn on one side of a mirror line is completed by reflective symmetry. What shape is formed?
mcqs.why: Example 3 in the notes flips the semicircle across the mirror line and draws the same part on the other side, completing it into a full circle.

mcqs.q: Which of these is given in the book as having rotational symmetry?
mcqs.why: The notes show a pedestal fan, tractor wheels and a circular table as shapes that look the same as they turn, so they have rotational symmetry.

mcqs.q: What is the order of symmetry of a shape?
options: The number of lines of symmetry it has
The number of times it looks the same in one full turn
The number of sides it has
The angle at which it is first turned
mcqs.why: The notes define the order of symmetry as the number of times a shape looks the same in one full turn about its centre of rotation.

mcqs.q: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a square?
mcqs.why: Example 4 rotates the square and shows it returns to its original position at the 4th rotation around 90 degrees, so its order of symmetry is 4.

mcqs.q: The rectangle and the letter S have rotational symmetry of which order?
mcqs.why: The notes state directly that the rectangle and the letter S have rotational symmetry of order 2, looking the same twice in one full turn.

mcqs.q: How many lines of symmetry does the letter P have?
mcqs.why: Exercise 9.3 Q3 states the letter P has no line of symmetry, because no mirror line divides it into two identical pieces.

mcqs.q: Which shape has exactly two lines of symmetry, as given in the notes?
mcqs.why: Exercise 9.3 Q4 gives a rectangle as the shape with exactly two lines of symmetry: the vertical and horizontal lines through its centre.

mcqs.q: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a five-pointed star?
mcqs.why: Exercise 9.3 Q8 states a five-pointed star has order 5 because it looks the same 5 times in one full turn around its centre.

lessons.title: 10.1 Construction of Line Segment
lessons.notes_html:
Introduction

Geometry is a branch of Mathematics. The word geometry comes from the Greek, which means “measurement of the earth.” It concerns the properties of points, straight lines, curved lines and surfaces of solids. “A line segment is a part of a line that is bounded by two distinct end points and contains every point on the line between its end points.” The part from A to B of a line is known as a line segment. It is denoted by AB.

Remember (book): A line is a series of points that extends in both directions without ends. A ray is a line with one end point.

We can draw a line segment by using compass and ruler. Look at the following examples.

Example 1 (Book) — Line Segment of 4 cm Using a Ruler

Draw a line segment mAB = 4 cm using a ruler. Steps of construction:

  1. Step I: Mark a point A on a paper.
  2. Step II: Place a ruler such that its zero point should be attached with point A.
  3. Step III: Mark another point B, 4 cm from point A by using the ruler.
  4. Step IV: Now, join points A and B together and then remove the ruler. mAB = 4 cm is the required line segment.

Example 2 (Book) — Line Segment of 5 cm Using a Compass

Draw a line segment of 5 cm using a compass. Steps of construction:

  1. Step I: Draw a ray AO on a paper.
  2. Step II: Place the needle of the compass at the ‘0’ of the ruler and open it 5 cm, as shown in the book.
  3. Step III: Place the needle of the compass at point A, then draw an arc of 5 cm on ray AO.
  4. Step IV: The arc cuts AO at B, so mAB = 5 cm is the required line segment.

Practice-1 (book): (i) Use your ruler to draw a line segment of 6 cm. (ii) Use your compass to draw a line segment of 9 cm. Follow exactly the steps of Example 1 for (i) and the steps of Example 2 for (ii), with the new lengths in place of 4 cm and 5 cm.

mcqs.q: The word 'geometry' comes from Greek. What does it mean?
mcqs.why: The notes state that geometry comes from the Greek and means 'measurement of the earth'; it deals with points, lines, curved lines and surfaces of solids.

mcqs.q: What is a line segment?
options: A line that extends forever in both directions
A curved part of a circle
A part of a line bounded by two distinct end points
A line with only one end point
mcqs.why: A line segment is a part of a line bounded by two distinct end points, and it contains every point on the line between those end points.

mcqs.q: The part of a line from point A to point B is denoted by which symbol?
mcqs.why: The notes say the part from A to B of a line is known as a line segment and it is denoted by AB, using its two end points.

mcqs.q: According to the notes, what is a line?
options: A part of a line between two end points
A series of points that extends in both directions without ends
A line with one end point
A closed shape with three sides
mcqs.why: The Remember box defines a line as a series of points that extends in both directions without ends, unlike a segment which has two end points.

mcqs.q: What is a ray?
options: A line segment of fixed length
A line that bends at one point
A line with one end point
mcqs.why: The Remember box defines a ray as a line with one end point; from that end point it extends in one direction, as with ray AO in Example 2.

mcqs.q: In Example 1, to draw a line segment of 4 cm with a ruler, where should the ruler's zero point be placed?
options: In the middle of the paper
At point B before B is marked
mcqs.why: Step II of Example 1 says to place the ruler such that its zero point is attached with point A, so distances are measured correctly from A.

mcqs.q: In Example 1, after placing the ruler's zero at A, what is done next to get mAB = 4 cm?
options: Draw an arc of 4 cm on a ray
Mark point B, 4 cm from point A, then join A and B
Draw a semi-circle centred at A
mcqs.why: Steps III and IV mark another point B, 4 cm from point A using the ruler, then join points A and B and remove the ruler to get mAB = 4 cm.

mcqs.q: What is the first step in Example 2 for drawing a line segment of 5 cm using a compass?
options: Draw a ray AO on a paper
Mark point B 5 cm from A with a ruler
Draw two arcs on both sides of AB
Join points A and B together
mcqs.why: Step I of Example 2 is to draw a ray AO on a paper; the compass arc is then drawn on this ray to cut off the required 5 cm length.

mcqs.q: In Example 2, how is the compass set to 5 cm before drawing the arc?
options: By guessing the opening of the compass
By placing the needle at point A and opening it freely
By drawing a semi-circle of radius 5 cm
By placing the needle at the '0' of the ruler and opening it 5 cm
mcqs.why: Step II places the needle of the compass at the '0' of the ruler and opens it 5 cm, so the compass opening exactly equals the required length.

mcqs.q: In Example 2, the arc drawn from A cuts ray AO at B. What length is mAB?
mcqs.why: Step IV states the arc cuts AO at B, so mAB = 5 cm is the required line segment, because the compass was opened to exactly 5 cm on the ruler.

lessons.title: 10.2 Perpendicular Bisector of a Line Segment
lessons.notes_html:
Perpendicular Bisector of a Line Segment

‘Bi’ means two and ‘section’ means part, so bisection means divide into two equal parts. The perpendicular bisector of a line segment is a line which makes a right angle with the given line segment and divides it into two equal parts. A perpendicular bisector always passes through the mid point of the line segment. It can be constructed by using a pair of compasses and a ruler. In the book's figure, line l is the perpendicular bisector of segment XY: it crosses XY at its mid point and the small square shows the right angle.

Example 3 (Book) — Perpendicular Bisector of mAB = 6 cm

Steps of construction:

  1. Step I: Draw mAB = 6 cm.
  2. Step II: Open the compass more than half of mAB. With centre at A, draw two arcs on both sides of AB.
  3. Step III: With centre at B, draw two arcs of the same radius cutting the previous arcs at L and M respectively.
  4. Step IV: Join L and M with a line cutting AB at point O; the angle at O is a right angle. So, LM is a perpendicular bisector of AB, and mAO = mOB = 3 cm.

Note (book): While drawing a perpendicular bisector, on the notebook only draw the step (iv) figure and write all the steps of construction. Remember: The perpendicular bisector is also known as the right bisector.

10.2.1 Difference Between Bisector and Perpendicular Bisector

Bisector: A bisector is a line that divides something, e.g. a line segment or an angle, into two equal parts.

Perpendicular bisector: A perpendicular bisector is a line that bisects a given line segment at a right angle. Also, it passes through the midpoint of the line segment.

10.2.2 Construction of a Perpendicular to a Given Line from a Point on It

Example 4 (Book) — Perpendicular to Line AB at a Given Point on AB

Steps of construction:

  1. Step I: Draw a line AB of given measurement and mark point X on the line.
  2. Step II: With the help of a compass, draw a semi-circle of any radius with centre at point X. This semi-circle touches line AB at points S and T respectively.
  3. Step III: Mark an arc above the line of any radius with centre at point S.
  4. Step IV: Now mark another arc above the line with the same radius centred at point T. This arc cuts the first arc at point Y.
  5. Step V: Now, join point Y with X. So, XY is the required perpendicular to AB at the given point X on it.

Practice-3 (book): Draw a line segment AB = 5 cm, then mark a point P on it and draw a perpendicular at this point — follow the five steps of Example 4 with P in place of X. Note (book): While drawing the bisector on the notebook, only draw the step (V) figure and write all the steps of construction.

10.2.3 Construction of a Perpendicular to a Given Line from a Point Outside the Line

Example 5 (Book) — Perpendicular from a Point X Outside the Line

Steps of construction:

  1. Step I: Draw AB of any measurement and mark point X above the line, as shown in the book.
  2. Step II: Draw an arc of any radius with centre at point X. The arc should cut the line at two points, say L and M.
  3. Step III: Mark a second arc of the same radius with centre at L (below the line).
  4. Step IV: Mark a third arc of the same radius with centre at M; this arc cuts the second arc at point Y.
  5. Step V: Join point X with Y, with line XY. So, XY is the required perpendicular to AB from a point X outside the line.

Practice-4 (book): Draw a perpendicular to the line segment mAB = 6 cm, from a point “P” that is outside the line — follow the five steps of Example 5. Note (book): While drawing a perpendicular on the notebook, only draw the step (V) figure and write all the points in the construction steps. Remember: A right bisector always intersects the given line at a right angle (90°). It can be checked by using a protractor.

Worked Examples — Exercise 10.1

The book's Answers section marks Exercise 10.1 as activity based; the full steps for every item are the book's own methods above, applied with the given measurements.

Q1. Draw line segments of the following measurements using ruler and compass: (i) 5 cm, (ii) 3.9 cm, (iii) 7 cm, (iv) 5.7 cm, (v) 6.5 cm. For each length, follow Example 1 (ruler): Step 1: Mark a point A on the paper. Step 2: Place the ruler with its zero point at A. Step 3: Mark point B at the given distance from A (5 cm, 3.9 cm, 7 cm, 5.7 cm or 6.5 cm). Step 4: Join A and B and remove the ruler; AB is the required segment. Or follow Example 2 (compass): draw a ray, open the compass to the given length on the ruler, place the needle at the starting point and cut the ray with an arc; the part up to the cut is the required segment.

Q2. Draw the right bisectors of the following line segments: (i) segment AB drawn in the book, (ii) segment PQ drawn in the book, (iii) segment XY drawn in the book, (iv) 7.8 cm, (v) 8 cm, (vi) 90 mm, (vii) 6.7 cm. For each segment, follow Example 3: Step 1: Draw the segment of the given measurement. Step 2: Open the compass more than half of the segment; with centre at the first end point, draw two arcs, one on each side of the segment. Step 3: With centre at the second end point and the same radius, draw two arcs cutting the previous arcs at two points. Step 4: Join those two points; the joining line is the right bisector (perpendicular bisector) — it cuts the segment at its mid point at a right angle.

Q3. Draw the perpendicular bisectors of the following line segments: (i) 7 cm, (ii) 6.8 cm, (iii) 8 mm, (iv) 92 mm, (v) 5.8 cm. Use exactly the four steps of Example 3 given for Q2, starting each time by drawing the segment of the given measurement.

Q4. Draw a perpendicular from the outside point on the following line segments: (i) 8.9 cm, (ii) 7.8 cm, (iii) 110 mm, (iv) 7 cm, (v) 9 cm. For each length, follow Example 5: Step 1: Draw the segment of the given measurement and mark a point above/outside the line. Step 2: With centre at that point, draw an arc cutting the line at two points L and M. Step 3: With centre at L, mark an arc of the same radius on the other side of the line. Step 4: With centre at M and the same radius, mark an arc cutting the previous arc at Y. Step 5: Join the outside point to Y; this line is the required perpendicular.

Q5. Draw mAB = 8 cm, mark a point outside it at some height over AB, then draw the perpendicular from that point to AB. Follow Example 5: draw AB = 8 cm; mark the point above AB; draw an arc centred at the point cutting AB at L and M; draw equal arcs centred at L and then at M so they cut each other at Y below AB; join the point to Y — the joining line is perpendicular to AB.

mcqs.q: The word 'bisection' comes from 'bi' meaning two and 'section' meaning part. What does bisection mean?
options: To divide into two equal parts
To divide into three equal parts
To make a right angle only
mcqs.why: The notes explain that 'bi' means two and 'section' means part, so bisection means to divide something into two equal parts.

mcqs.q: What is the perpendicular bisector of a line segment?
options: A line parallel to the segment
A line which makes a right angle with the segment and divides it into two equal parts
A line joining the two end points
A line that bisects an angle only
mcqs.why: The perpendicular bisector makes a right angle with the given line segment and divides it into two equal parts, passing through its mid point.

mcqs.q: Through which point does a perpendicular bisector always pass?
options: One end point of the segment
The mid point of the line segment
mcqs.why: The notes state that a perpendicular bisector always passes through the mid point of the line segment, where it meets the segment at a right angle.

mcqs.q: By what other name is the perpendicular bisector known?
mcqs.why: The book's Remember note says the perpendicular bisector is also known as the right bisector, because it bisects the segment at a right angle.

mcqs.q: In Example 3 (perpendicular bisector of mAB = 6 cm), how much should the compass be opened in Step II?
options: Equal to the whole of mAB
mcqs.why: Step II says to open the compass more than half of mAB; only then will arcs drawn from A and from B meet each other on both sides of AB.

mcqs.q: In Example 3, the arcs drawn from centres A and B cut each other at which two points?
mcqs.why: Step III draws arcs from centre B with the same radius cutting the previous arcs at L and M respectively; joining L and M gives the bisector.

mcqs.q: In Example 3, LM cuts AB at O. If mAB = 6 cm, what are mAO and mOB?
mcqs.why: LM is the perpendicular bisector, so O is the mid point: mAO = mOB = 6 cm / 2 = 3 cm, and the angle at O is a right angle.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a bisector and a perpendicular bisector?
options: A bisector divides into two equal parts, while a perpendicular bisector also bisects at a right angle through the midpoint
There is no difference at all
A perpendicular bisector never divides into equal parts
A bisector always makes a right angle, a perpendicular bisector never does
mcqs.why: A bisector simply divides something into two equal parts, but a perpendicular bisector bisects a line segment at a right angle and passes through its midpoint.

mcqs.q: In Example 4 (perpendicular at a point X on line AB), the semi-circle drawn with centre X touches line AB at which points?
mcqs.why: Step II of Example 4 draws a semi-circle of any radius with centre at X, and this semi-circle touches line AB at points S and T respectively.

mcqs.q: In Example 5, to draw a perpendicular from a point X outside line AB, the first arc drawn with centre X must cut the line at how many points?
options: Two points, say L and M
mcqs.why: Step II of Example 5 draws an arc with centre at X that cuts the line at two points, L and M; equal arcs from L and M then locate point Y for line XY.

lessons.title: 10.3 Construction of Angles
lessons.notes_html:
What is an Angle?

If a person raises the screen of a laptop slowly, the edge rises and creates a gap between the screen and the base. If the screen is raised higher, the two sides remain joined at one end and the space between the other two ends is increased. The book shows laptop screens open at 110°, 60° and 90°. So, an angle refers to the space between two surfaces or intersecting lines at the point where they meet. In previous classes, we have learnt the construction of angles of different measures using a protractor. Now, we will learn the construction of an angle by using the pair of compasses.

10.3.1 Construction of an Angle Equal in Measure to a Given Angle

Example 6 (Book) — Construct m∠AOB = 60° (Copy a Given Angle)

We can construct an angle equal in measure to a given angle using a compass. The given angle is m∠AOB = 60°. Steps of construction:

  1. Step I: Draw ray PQ of any suitable measurement, as shown in the book.
  2. Step II: Draw an arc of any radius with centre at point O. This arc cuts OA at point ‘S’ and OB at point T.
  3. Step III: With centre ‘P’, draw an arc of radius equal to mOS to cut PQ at point X.
  4. Step IV: Now, place the compass on S and take the measurement of arc ST, as given.
  5. Step V: Place the needle at point X and draw another arc which cuts the first arc at point Y.
  6. Step VI: Now, draw ray PR which is passing through point Y. m∠QPR is the required angle. Hence, m∠QPR = m∠AOB = 60°.

Note (book): While constructing an angle of a given angle's measurement, only draw the step (VI) figure using the above steps and write all the steps of construction.

10.3.2 Construction of an Angle Twice in Measure of a Given Angle

Example 7 (Book) — Construct an Angle Twice m∠AOB = 60°

Steps of construction:

  1. Step I: Follow the method used in Example 6, Steps (I–V), for the construction of m∠QPR.
  2. Step II: Now, draw another arc with centre at point Y having the same radius. This arc cuts the first arc at point Z, as shown in the book.
  3. Step III: Now, draw ray PR which is passing through point Z. The angle m∠QPR = 120° is the required angle (twice 60°).

Note (book): While constructing a double angle of a given angle's measurement on the notebook, only draw the step (iii) figure and write all the points in the construction steps.

10.3.3 Use Compass to Bisect a Given Angle

Bisection of an angle means to divide the given angle into two equal angles. Remember (book): Bisector of an angle means division of a given angle into two equal parts.

Example 8 (Book) — Bisector of m∠AOB = 60°

Steps of construction:

  1. Step I: Draw an arc of any radius at point ‘O’, which cuts OA at point X and OB at point Y.
  2. Step II: Now, with centre at point X, draw an arc of any radius, as shown in the book.
  3. Step III: With centre at point Y, draw another arc of the same radius which cuts the first arc at point Z.
  4. Step IV: Now, join point O with Z and draw ray OZ. So, OZ is the required angle bisector (each part is 30°).

Note (book): While bisecting a given angle on the notebook, only draw the figure in step (IV) and write all the other steps in the construction steps. Practice-6 (book): Divide ∠AOB = 75° (as drawn in the book) into two equal angles — follow the four steps of Example 8; each part is 37.5°.

10.3.4 Construction of Angles

The method of construction of different types of angles using a compass is illustrated in the following examples. Remember (book): An angle of 60° is a basic angle in the construction of angles.

Construction of Angle 60° — Example 9 (Book)

Construct an angle of 60° with the help of a compass. Steps of construction:

  1. Step I: Draw ray OA of any measurement.
  2. Step II: With centre at point O, draw an arc of any radius, which cuts OA at point X.
  3. Step III: Now, draw a second arc of the same radius with centre at point X, which cuts the first arc at point Y.
  4. Step IV: Join point Y with point O and draw ray OB. Hence, m∠AOB = 60° is the required angle.

Construction of Angle 30° — Example 9 (Book, as numbered)

Construct m∠AOB = 30° using a compass. As 60° ÷ 2 = 30°, first construct angle 60° and then bisect it. Steps of construction:

  1. Step I: Use all the steps of the 60° construction and construct m∠AOC = 60°, as shown in the book (C is the ray making 60° with OA, and Y is the point where the arcs cut).
  2. Step II: With centre at point X, mark an arc of any radius, as shown in the book.
  3. Step III: Now draw a third arc with centre at point Y of the same radius. The third arc cuts the second arc at point Z.
  4. Step IV: Join point Z with point O, and draw ray OB. Hence, m∠AOB = 30° is the required angle.

Remember (book): m∠AOB = m∠BOC = 30° and m∠AOB + m∠BOC = 60°.

Construction of Angle 90° — Example 10 (Book)

Draw m∠AOB = 90° using a compass. Steps of construction:

  1. Step I: Draw ray OA, as shown in the book.
  2. Step II: Draw an arc of any radius with centre at point O, as shown in the book, which cuts OA at point X.
  3. Step III: Draw the second arc with centre at X, cutting the previous arc at Y. Draw the third arc with centre at point Y, cutting the first arc at point Z.
  4. Step IV: Draw a fourth arc of any radius with centre at point Y.
  5. Step V: Now, with centre at point Z, draw a fifth arc of the same radius as in step IV, which cuts the fourth arc at point S, as shown in the book.
  6. Step VI: Join point S with O and draw ray OB. Hence, m∠AOB = 90° is the required angle.

Construction of Angle 45° — Example 11 (Book)

Construct m∠AOB = 45° using a compass. As 90° ÷ 2 = 45°, construct angle 90° then bisect it. Steps of construction:

  1. Step I: Use all the steps of Example 10 and construct an angle of 90° where ray OC passes through the point ‘T’.
  2. Step II: Draw an arc of any radius with centre at point X, as shown in the book.
  3. Step III: Now, with centre at point T, draw another arc with the previous radius which cuts the first arc at point U.
  4. Step IV: Join point U with O and draw ray OB. Hence, m∠AOB = 45° is the required angle.

Remember (book): m∠AOB = m∠BOC = 45° and m∠AOB + m∠BOC = 90°. Note (book): We bisect the angle between 60° and 90° for the next construction, using the fact (60° + 90°) ÷ 2 = 75°.

Construction of Angle 75° — Example 12 (Book)

Construct an angle of 75° using a compass. Steps of construction:

  1. Step I: Use all the steps of Example 10 to construct an angle of 90°, where ray OC is passing through the point T.
  2. Step II: With the centre at point Y, draw an arc of any radius, as shown in the book.
  3. Step III: Now, with the centre at point T, draw another arc with the previous radius which cuts the first arc at point U.
  4. Step IV: Join point U with O and draw ray OB. Hence, m∠AOB = 75° is the required angle.

Construction of Angle 120° — Example 13 (Book)

Construct an angle of m∠AOB = 120° using a compass. As 60° + 60° = 120°, construct an angle of 60° twice to get an angle of 120°. Steps of construction:

  1. Step I: Draw ray OA. Then, with centre at point O, mark a long arc of any radius which cuts OA at point X.
  2. Step II: Draw another arc of the previous radius with centre at point X, which cuts the first arc at point Y.
  3. Step III: Now, draw the third arc of the same radius with centre at point Y, which cuts the first arc at point Z.
  4. Step IV: Join point Z with point O and draw ray OB. Hence, m∠AOB = 120° is the required angle.

Construction of Angle 105° — Example 14 (Book)

Construct m∠AOB = 105° by using a compass. As 90° + 15° = 105°, construct an angle of 90° and bisect the angle between 90° and 120°. Steps of construction:

  1. Step I: Use all the steps of Example 10 and Example 13 to construct angles of 90° and 120° respectively.
  2. Step II: Draw an arc of any radius with centre at point Z, as shown in the book (Z is the 120° point on the arc and T is the 90° point).
  3. Step III: Now, draw another arc of the same radius with centre at point T, which cuts the previous arc at U.
  4. Step IV: Join point U with point O and draw ray OB. Hence, m∠AOB = 105° is the required angle.

Remember (book): As m∠AOC = 90° and m∠COB = 15°, so m∠AOC + m∠COB = 105°.

Worked Examples — Exercise 10.2

The book's Answers section marks Exercise 10.2 as activity based; use the book's bisection steps (Example 8) and angle constructions (Examples 9–14) as follows.

Q1. Bisect the following angles — for each angle, follow Example 8: draw an arc centred at the vertex cutting both arms; draw equal arcs centred at those two cut points so they cross inside the angle; join the vertex to the crossing point. The bisector divides the angle into two equal parts:

  • (i) The angle of 55° drawn in the book (∠XOY): each part = 55° ÷ 2 = 27.5°.
  • (ii) The angle of 70° drawn in the book (∠ABC): each part = 70° ÷ 2 = 35°.
  • (iii) The angle drawn in the book at point O: bisect it by the same four steps; the two parts are equal.
  • (iv) 90°: each part = 45°.
  • (v) 80°: each part = 40°.
  • (vi) 120°: each part = 60°.

Q2. Construct the following angles using a compass: (i) 30° — construct 60° (Example 9) and bisect it, as in the 30° construction. (ii) 60° — follow Example 9 directly. (iii) 120° — follow Example 13 (60° twice). (iv) 90° — follow Example 10. (v) 45° — construct 90° and bisect it (Example 11). (vi) 75° — construct 90° and bisect the angle between 60° and 90° (Example 12). (vii) 105° — construct 90° and 120° and bisect the angle between them (Example 14). (viii) 150° — construct 90° (Example 10) and then, from the 90° ray, construct a further 60° by the arc method of Example 9 beside it, so the total angle from the starting ray is 90° + 60° = 150°.

mcqs.q: According to the notes, what is an angle?
options: The space between two surfaces or intersecting lines at the point where they meet
The length of a line segment
A closed shape with three sides
The distance between two parallel lines
mcqs.why: Using the laptop screen example, the notes define an angle as the space between two surfaces or intersecting lines at the point where they meet.

mcqs.q: Which angle is called the basic angle in the construction of angles?
mcqs.why: The Remember box states that an angle of 60 degrees is a basic angle in the construction of angles; 30 degrees and 120 degrees are both built from it.

mcqs.q: In Example 6, a copy of the given angle mAOB = 60 degrees is constructed as angle QPR. What is mQPR?
mcqs.why: Example 6 copies the given angle exactly using arcs of the same radii, so the constructed angle satisfies mQPR = mAOB = 60 degrees.

mcqs.q: In Example 7, an angle twice the measure of mAOB = 60 degrees is constructed. What is the resulting angle?
mcqs.why: Twice the given angle is 2 x 60 degrees = 120 degrees; a second arc of the same radius from Y locates point Z, giving mQPR = 120 degrees.

mcqs.q: In Example 8, angle AOB = 60 degrees is bisected by ray OZ. How big is each part?
mcqs.why: Bisection divides the angle into two equal parts, so each part is 60 degrees / 2 = 30 degrees, as stated at the end of Example 8.

mcqs.q: Following Example 8, if angle AOB = 75 degrees is bisected, what is the measure of each equal part?
mcqs.why: Practice-6 bisects 75 degrees into two equal angles, so each part is 75 degrees / 2 = 37.5 degrees, using the four steps of Example 8.

mcqs.q: How is an angle of 30 degrees constructed with a compass?
options: By copying a 30 degree angle with a protractor
By constructing 60 degrees and then bisecting it
By constructing 120 degrees and halving it twice only
mcqs.why: Since 60 degrees / 2 = 30 degrees, the notes first construct a 60 degree angle and then bisect it; the bisector gives mAOB = 30 degrees.

mcqs.q: How is an angle of 45 degrees constructed in Example 11?
options: By constructing 90 degrees and then bisecting it
By bisecting the angle between 60 and 90 degrees
mcqs.why: As 90 degrees / 2 = 45 degrees, Example 11 constructs a 90 degree angle first and then bisects it, giving mAOB = mBOC = 45 degrees.

mcqs.q: An angle of 75 degrees is obtained by bisecting the angle between 60 degrees and 90 degrees. Which calculation shows this?
mcqs.why: The book's note uses (60 degrees + 90 degrees) / 2 = 75 degrees: bisecting the angle between the 60 degree and 90 degree rays gives the 75 degree ray.

mcqs.q: In Example 14, an angle of 105 degrees is constructed. Which pair of angles is bisected to get it?
options: The angles of 60 degrees and 90 degrees
The angles of 30 degrees and 60 degrees
The angles of 45 degrees and 90 degrees
The angles of 90 degrees and 120 degrees
mcqs.why: Example 14 constructs 90 degrees and 120 degrees and bisects the angle between them, giving 90 degrees + 15 degrees = 105 degrees, so mAOB = 105 degrees.

lessons.title: 10.4 Finding Unknown Angles of a Straight Line and Triangle
lessons.notes_html:
Triangles — Introduction

In our previous classes, we have learnt about triangles: “A polygon with three straight edges and three angles is known as a triangle.” In the book's figure, polygon XYZ is a triangle having three sides XY, YZ, XZ and three angles ∠X, ∠Y and ∠Z respectively. In this section, we will learn different methods to find the unknown angles in a triangle (interior and exterior angles). Remember (book): A polygon is a closed shape which has three or more straight edges.

10.4.1 Finding of Unknown Angles — Types of Angles

  • (i) Acute angle: An angle which is less than 90° is called an acute angle, e.g. m∠AOB = 55°.
  • (ii) Right angle: An angle which is equal to 90° is called a right angle, e.g. m∠XOL = 90°.
  • (iii) Obtuse angle: An angle which is greater than 90° is called an obtuse angle, e.g. m∠POQ = 110°.
  • (iv) Straight angle: An angle which is equal to 180° is called a straight angle, e.g. m∠AOB = 180°.
  • (v) Reflex angle: An angle which is greater than 180° but less than 360° is called a reflex angle, e.g. m∠XOY = 225°.
  • (vi) Complete angle: An angle which is equal to 360° is called a complete angle, e.g. ∠O = 360°.

(i) Complementary angles: If the sum of two angles is 90°, then the angles are called complementary angles, e.g. 30° + 60° = 90°.

(ii) Supplementary angles: If the sum of two angles is 180°, then the angles are called supplementary angles, e.g. 140° + 40° = 180°.

(iii) Adjacent angles: Two angles are said to be adjacent angles if they have a common vertex, they have a common arm, and they lie on opposite sides of the common arm. e.g. ∠AOC and ∠BOC are adjacent angles; OC is the common arm and O is the common vertex.

Example 15 (Book) — Unknown Angles on a Straight Line

Find the value of the unknown angles in the following figures. Solution:

  • (i) 135° + x = 180° (supplementary angles), so x = 180° − 135°, therefore x = 45°.
  • (ii) 80° + x + 37° = 180° (supplementary angles), so x + 117° = 180°, x = 180° − 117°, therefore x = 63°.

Practice-9 (book): Find the value of the unknown angles in the given figure, using the same rule: angles on a straight line are supplementary and add to 180°.

10.4.2 Triangles — Types With Respect to Sides

  • (i) Equilateral triangle: A triangle of which all three sides are equal is called an equilateral triangle, e.g. △ABC is an equilateral triangle. All the angles in an equilateral triangle are 60°.
  • (ii) Isosceles triangle: A triangle with 2 equal sides is called an isosceles triangle, e.g. △XYZ is an isosceles triangle. Two angles of an isosceles triangle are always equal.
  • (iii) Scalene triangle: A triangle of which all three sides are different is called a scalene triangle, e.g. △LMN is a scalene triangle. All angles of a scalene triangle are different.

Remember (book): The sum of all interior angles of any triangle is always equal to 180°.

Types of Triangle With Respect to Angles

  • (i) Acute triangle: A triangle of which all 3 interior angles are acute angles is called an acute angled triangle, e.g. △ABC.
  • (ii) Obtuse triangle: A triangle of which 1 interior angle is an obtuse angle is called an obtuse angled triangle, e.g. △XYZ.
  • (iii) Right triangle: A triangle of which 1 interior angle is a right angle is called a right angled triangle, e.g. △LMN (the right angle is at M, marked with a small square).

Exterior Angles of a Triangle

Observe the triangle LMN in the book: ∠a, ∠b and ∠c are the interior angles of △LMN, and ∠x, ∠y and ∠z are the exterior angles of △LMN. “An angle which is formed by any side of a triangle and the extension of its adjacent side is called an exterior angle.” In the book's figure, side LM is extended to form ∠x, MN is extended to form ∠y, and NL is extended to form ∠z.

Fun Fact (book): (i) An exterior angle is equal to the sum of the two opposite interior angles. (ii) The sum of all exterior angles of any triangle is always equal to 360°; in △LMN, x + y + z = 360°.

Example 16 (Book) — Finding x in Triangles

Solution:

  • (i) x is an exterior angle with opposite interior angles 38° and 67°, so x = 38° + 67° = 105° (sum of two opposite interior angles).
  • (ii) First find t: t + 43° + 56° = 180° (sum of interior angles of a triangle), so t = 180° − 43° − 56° = 81°. Then x is an exterior angle of the second triangle with opposite interior angles 35° and t, so x = 35° + 81° = 116° (sum of opposite interior angles).

Worked Examples — Exercise 10.3

Q1. Find the value of the unknown angles:

  • (i) x° and 126° are on a straight line, so x = 180° − 126° = 54°.
  • (ii) 47°, x° and 41° are on a straight line, so x = 180° − 47° − 41° = 92°.
  • (iii) x° and 42° are complementary (they make a right angle with the vertical line), so x = 90° − 42° = 48°.

Q2. The measurement of two angles is 89° and 107°. Do these angles form a straight line? 89° + 107° = 196°, which is not 180°. Answer: No — angles on a straight line must add to 180°.

Q3. The measurement of four angles is 83°, 142°, 34° and 63°. Which three angles form a straight line? 83° + 63° + 34° = 180°, so the three angles 83°, 63° and 34° form a straight line.

Q4. Find the value of x and y in the following figures (answers as given in the book's Answers section):

  • (i) x = 132°, y = 35° (x is supplementary to 48°: 180° − 48° = 132°; y is supplementary to 145°: 180° − 145° = 35°).
  • (ii) x = 57°, y = 43° (x = 180° − 123° = 57°; y = 180° − 137° = 43°).
  • (iii) x = 15°, y = 156° (x = 180° − 165° = 15°; y = 180° − 24° = 156°).

Q5. Find the value of x in the following figures (answers as given in the book's Answers section):

  • (i) x is an exterior angle, equal to the sum of the two opposite interior angles: x = 66° + 63° = 129°.
  • (ii) x is an exterior angle, equal to the sum of the two opposite interior angles: x = 80° + 50° = 130°.
  • (iii) The two base interior angles are 45° and 48° (vertically opposite to the marked exterior angles), so x = 180° − 45° − 48° = 87°.
  • (iv) Using the sum of interior angles of a triangle (180°), x = 68°.

Q6. Calculate all the interior and exterior angles of an equilateral triangle. All the angles in an equilateral triangle are 60°, so each interior angle = 60°. Each exterior angle = 180° − 60° = 120°.

Q7. Find the size of each interior angle of a regular 3-sided polygon. A regular 3-sided polygon is an equilateral triangle, so each interior angle = 60°.

mcqs.q: An angle of 55 degrees, like mAOB in the notes, is an example of which type of angle?
mcqs.why: An angle which is less than 90 degrees is called an acute angle, and the notes give mAOB = 55 degrees as the example of an acute angle.

mcqs.q: An angle of 225 degrees, like mXOY in the notes, is which type of angle?
mcqs.why: A reflex angle is greater than 180 degrees but less than 360 degrees, and the notes give mXOY = 225 degrees as the example of a reflex angle.

mcqs.q: Two angles measuring 30 degrees and 60 degrees are called complementary angles because their sum is what?
mcqs.why: If the sum of two angles is 90 degrees, the angles are called complementary angles; the notes give the example 30 degrees + 60 degrees = 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: On a straight line, one angle is 135 degrees and the other is x. Find x.
mcqs.why: Angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees, so 135 + x = 180, giving x = 180 - 135 = 45 degrees; the two angles are supplementary.

mcqs.q: Three angles on a straight line are 80 degrees, x and 37 degrees. Find x.
mcqs.why: Angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees, so 80 + x + 37 = 180, giving x + 117 = 180 and x = 180 - 117 = 63 degrees.

mcqs.q: In a triangle, two interior angles are 43 degrees and 56 degrees, and the third angle is t. Find t.
mcqs.why: Triangle angles sum to 180 degrees, so t + 43 + 56 = 180, giving t = 180 - 43 - 56 = 81 degrees, as worked in Example 16.

mcqs.q: An exterior angle of a triangle has opposite interior angles of 38 degrees and 67 degrees. Find the exterior angle x.
mcqs.why: Triangle angles sum to 180 degrees and angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees, so an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles: x = 38 + 67 = 105 degrees.

mcqs.q: Each interior angle of an equilateral triangle is 60 degrees. What is each exterior angle?
mcqs.why: Angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees, so each exterior angle = 180 - 60 = 120 degrees; the interior angles also satisfy the triangle angles sum to 180 degrees: 60 + 60 + 60 = 180.

mcqs.q: What is an isosceles triangle?
options: A triangle with all three sides equal
A triangle with all three sides different
A triangle with one right angle
mcqs.why: The notes define an isosceles triangle as a triangle with 2 equal sides, and they add that two angles of an isosceles triangle are always equal.

mcqs.q: Two angles measure 89 degrees and 107 degrees. Do they form a straight line?
options: Yes, because their sum is 180 degrees
No, because their sum is 196 degrees, not 180 degrees
Yes, because both are obtuse or acute
No, because their sum is 180 degrees
mcqs.why: Angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees, but 89 + 107 = 196 degrees, which is not 180 degrees, so these angles do not form a straight line.

chapters.title: Unit 11: Statistics and Probability — Sub-Domain 1: Data Management

lessons.title: 11.1 GROUPED AND UNGROUPED DATA
lessons.notes_html:
Introduction — Data

In our previous classes, we have learnt about data. Data is a collection of any information and facts, such as numbers, words, measurements, observations or even description of things.

Numerical data or information is very valuable because it helps us to understand the changes which take place in our daily lives. For example, numerical data or information about temperature helps us to know the condition of water. We can collect the data by several ways i.e. surveys, interviews, observation and questionnaire, etc.

Remember: A survey is a method of collecting information/data about a group.

The frequency of an event is the number of times the event occurred in an information or study or data.

Ungrouped data

Most surveys or observations produce a large amount of numerical data. It is so complicated to draw the meaningful conclusion from large range of numerical data. To make the meaningful results of data collection, the data is classified into two groups/categories.

The data which provides us information or data points individually is known as ungrouped data.

Example 1: The following table shows the scores of Pakistan cricket team in a one day international cricket match. The runs of each player are showing.

Name of playersSarfarazUmarHafeezShoaibYasirAmirKamranShahidFaheemWaseemWaqar
Runs1925154580207189285

Grouped data

The data which is given in intervals or groups provide us the information about the data.

In the above example, the runs of the players can be organized into the following classes or groups or intervals: 0 − 19, 20 − 39, 40 − 59, 60 − 79, 80 − 99.

The below frequency table shows the runs of the players in groups or classes.

RunsTally markFrequency
0 − 195 + 1 (six tally marks)6
20 − 39III3
40 − 59I1
60 − 79—0
80 − 99I1

Activity-1: Ask the obtained marks of class-5 result of your all classfellows and show the result in grouped and ungrouped tables.

Worked examples — Exercise 11.1

Q.1 Define the following: Data, Ungrouped data, Grouped data.

Step 1: Data — Data is a collection of any information and facts, such as numbers, words, measurements, observations or even description of things.

Step 2: Ungrouped data — The data which provides us information or data points individually is known as ungrouped data.

Step 3: Grouped data — The data which is given in intervals or groups is called grouped data.

Final answer: Data is a collection of information and facts; data given individually is ungrouped data; data given in intervals or groups is grouped data.
