mcqs.q: What is data, according to the lesson?
options: Only a list of numbers obtained in a survey
A collection of information and facts, such as numbers, words, measurements, observations or descriptions of things
Only the measurements recorded in an experiment
A table in which values are arranged in intervals
mcqs.why: The lesson defines data as a collection of any information and facts, including numbers, words, measurements, observations and descriptions of things.

mcqs.q: What is a survey?
options: A method of collecting information or data about a group
A table showing frequencies in intervals
The number of times an event occurs
A graph drawn from collected information
mcqs.why: The lesson states: a survey is a method of collecting information/data about a group. Surveys, interviews, observation and questionnaires are ways to collect data.

mcqs.q: The frequency of an event is:
options: The interval in which the event falls
The total number of events in the whole study only
The number of times the event occurred in the information, study or data
The name given to a group of data values
mcqs.why: Frequency means how many times the event occurred. For example, if a value appears six times in the data, its frequency is 6.

mcqs.q: Data which provides information or data points individually is called:
mcqs.why: Ungrouped data gives each data point individually, for example the age of each named student listed one by one in a table.

mcqs.q: Data which is given in intervals or groups is called:
mcqs.why: Grouped data is presented in intervals or groups, such as marks arranged in the classes 1-20, 21-40, 41-60 and so on, with a frequency for each class.

mcqs.q: A table lists the ages of students individually: Aliya 10, Shumaila 15, Samreen 8, Sameen 7, Aleezay 16, Laiba 11, Arsheena 10. This table shows:
options: Grouped data, because ages are numbers
Ungrouped data, because each student's age is given individually
Grouped data, because there are seven students
mcqs.why: Each student's age is written separately against her name, with no intervals or classes used, so the data is ungrouped data.

mcqs.q: A table shows obtained marks of grade 6 students as: 1-20 (frequency 5), 21-40 (10), 41-60 (12), 61-80 (21), 81-100 (25). This table shows:
options: Ungrouped data, because individual marks are listed
Ungrouped data, because frequencies are given
Grouped data, because the marks are given in intervals with frequencies
Survey data only, not grouped data
mcqs.why: The marks are not listed one by one; they are placed in the intervals 1-20, 21-40, 41-60, 61-80 and 81-100, so this is grouped data.

mcqs.q: In the grouped table of Pakistan cricket team runs (0-19: 6, 20-39: 3, 40-59: 1, 60-79: 0, 80-99: 1), what is the frequency of the class 0-19?
mcqs.why: The frequency table records six tally marks for the class 0-19, so its frequency is 6, meaning six players scored between 0 and 19 runs.

mcqs.q: Using the same grouped runs table (0-19: 6, 20-39: 3, 40-59: 1, 60-79: 0, 80-99: 1), how many players are recorded in the table altogether?
mcqs.why: Total frequency = 6 + 3 + 1 + 0 + 1 = 11. Adding the frequencies of all classes gives the total number of players, which is 11.

mcqs.q: A table shows the distance covered by a bus each day individually: Monday 150 km, Tuesday 95 km, Wednesday 215 km, Thursday 317 km, Friday 415 km, Saturday 210 km, Sunday 125 km. This is:
options: Grouped data, because distances are large numbers
Ungrouped data, because the distance for each day is given individually
Grouped data, because a full week is covered
mcqs.why: One separate distance is given for each named day and no intervals or classes are used, so the bus distance table is ungrouped data.

lessons.title: 11.2 CONTINUOUS AND DISCRETE VARIABLES
lessons.notes_html:
Types of variables

We are familiar about variable that a variable is a quantity whose value changes. Here, we will discuss two types of variables: Discrete variables and Continuous variables.

(i) Discrete variables

“A variable whose values are obtained by counting is called discrete variable.” For example:

  • Blue marbles in the jar.
  • Number of tails when flipping a coin.
  • Number of children in a family.

(ii) Continuous variables

“A variable whose value is obtained by measurement is called continuous variable.” For example:

  • Height of a student of grade 6 is 5 feet.
  • Distance from a city to another city is 25.3 km.
  • Mass of student is 49.7 kg.

Activity-2: Observe in your surrounding and give at least three examples of discrete variables and three of continuous variables.

Worked examples — Exercise 11.1

Q.3 For each of the following, write discrete variable or continuous variable. (i) Number of people in a school. (ii) Mass of a mobile. (iii) Number of pages in your Mathematics book. (iv) The size of your shoe. (v) The volume of your water bottle. (vi) The number of players in football team.

Step 1: (i) Number of people is obtained by counting, so it is a discrete variable.

Step 2: (ii) Mass of a mobile is obtained by measurement, so it is a continuous variable.

Step 3: (iii) Number of pages is obtained by counting, so it is a discrete variable.

Step 4: (iv) The size of a shoe is obtained by measurement, so it is a continuous variable.

Step 5: (v) The volume of a water bottle is obtained by measurement, so it is a continuous variable.

Step 6: (vi) The number of players is obtained by counting, so it is a discrete variable.

Final answer: (i) Discrete variable (ii) Continuous variable (iii) Discrete variable (iv) Continuous variable (v) Continuous variable (vi) Discrete variable.

Q.4 A school keeps the record of blood groups of all students who donate blood every year. Is that record a discrete variable or continuous variable?

Step 1: Recall the book's rule: a variable whose values are obtained by counting is discrete, and a variable whose value is obtained by measurement is continuous.

Step 2: The book's Answers section records this item as a continuous variable.

Final answer: Continuous variable (as given in the book's Answers).

Practice-1: Count total number of trees and students in your school. Arrange your data in the form of grouped or ungrouped data. Which type of variable you need to use for your data?

mcqs.q: A variable is:
options: A quantity whose value never changes
Only a number obtained by measurement
Only a number obtained by counting
mcqs.why: The lesson begins by recalling that a variable is a quantity whose value changes; it is then classified as discrete or continuous.

mcqs.q: A discrete variable is a variable whose values are obtained by:
mcqs.why: By definition, a variable whose values are obtained by counting is a discrete variable, such as the number of children in a family.

mcqs.q: A continuous variable is a variable whose value is obtained by:
mcqs.why: By definition, a variable whose value is obtained by measurement is continuous, for example a height of 5 feet or a mass of 49.7 kg.

mcqs.q: The number of people in a school is an example of:
options: A continuous variable, because a school is large
A discrete variable, because the number of people is obtained by counting
A continuous variable, because people have different heights
mcqs.why: People are counted one by one, not measured, so the number of people in a school is a discrete variable.

mcqs.q: The mass of a mobile phone is an example of:
mcqs.why: Mass is found with a measuring instrument such as a balance, so the mass of a mobile is obtained by measurement and is a continuous variable.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a discrete variable?
options: The number of pages in your Mathematics book
The volume of your water bottle
The mass of a student, 49.7 kg
The distance between two cities, 25.3 km
mcqs.why: Pages are counted, so the number of pages is discrete. Volume, mass and distance are all obtained by measurement, so they are continuous.

mcqs.q: The size of your shoe is classified in the lesson as:
options: A discrete variable, because shoes are counted in pairs
A discrete variable, because it is a whole number
A continuous variable, because it is obtained by measurement
mcqs.why: Shoe size comes from measuring the foot, and the lesson classifies the size of a shoe as a continuous variable because it is obtained by measurement.

mcqs.q: The number of tails when flipping a coin is an example of:
mcqs.why: Tails are counted as they occur when the coin is flipped; values obtained by counting give a discrete variable, as in the lesson's examples.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a continuous variable?
options: Number of children in a family
Height of a grade 6 student, 5 feet
Number of players in a football team
mcqs.why: Height is obtained by measurement, so it is continuous. Marbles, children and players are all counted, so those variables are discrete.

mcqs.q: The number of players in a football team is:
options: A continuous variable, because players run different distances
A continuous variable, because it is measured during a match
A discrete variable, because the number of players is obtained by counting
mcqs.why: Players are counted one by one; a variable whose values are obtained by counting is a discrete variable, as the lesson's exercise confirms.

lessons.title: 11.3 GRAPHS
lessons.notes_html:
Graphs

Have you seen the graphs around you, like in the newspapers, television, magazines and books etc? The purpose of graph is to show numerical facts in visual form, so that it can be understood quickly, easily and clearly.

“A graph is a diagram representing a system of connections or interrelations among two or more things by a number of lines, pictures, distinctive dots and bars, etc.”

We use a graph to display a data in a simple and attractive way. There are different types of graphs such as pictograph, line graph, bar graph and multiple bar graph.

11.3.1 A Bar Graph

“A bar graph is a graphical display of data using bars of different heights.”

There are two types of bar graphs: Horizontal bar graph and Vertical bar graph.

Remember: A bar graph is also known as bar chart.

Note: Always choose a scale that allows all the data to be represented clearly in the available space.

The book shows a horizontal bar graph of the mass of grade 6 students (names of students on the Y-axis, mass of students on the X-axis) and a vertical bar graph of the obtained marks of students in a class test: Naseem 3, Ahmed 10, Rabia 6, Sobia 7, Qaiser 5, Saima 5, Nida 9.

Simple bar graphs — Example 2

Example 2: The students of different classes in a school were asked that how many of students had read the storybooks in summer vacation. The results are shown in the following table. Show this result in horizontal bar graph.

Name of classIIIIVVVIVIIVIIIIXX
Number of students834591056

Steps of drawing a horizontal bar graph:

Step 1: Draw two lines XX′ and YY′ on a graph paper. Both lines are perpendicular to each other and cut at point ‘0’. The horizontal line is called X-axis and the vertical line is called Y-axis.

Step 2: Give the title as “Horizontal bar graph for number of students in each class.”

Step 3: Label X-axis as ‘Number of students’ and Y-axis as ‘Name of classes’.

Step 4: Make a scale for each axis (on X-axis each large square box = 1 student and on Y-axis each large square box represents a class).

Step 5: Make bars of equal width at equal distance on Y-axis according to the given data: III = 8, IV = 3, V = 4, VI = 5, VII = 9, VIII = 10, IX = 5, X = 6.

Simple bar graphs — Example 3

Example 3: Given below are the seats won by different political parties in the polling outcome of a national assembly election 2018. Draw a vertical bar graph to represent the polling results.

Political partiesABCDEF
Seats won805536251030

Steps of drawing a vertical bar graph:

Step 1: Draw two lines XX′ and YY′ on a graph paper. Both lines are perpendicular to each other and cut at point ‘0’. The horizontal line is called X-axis and the vertical line is called Y-axis.

Step 2: Give the graph title (vertical bar graph for polling results of 2018 election).

Step 3: Label X-axis as “political parties” and Y-axis as “number of seats won”.

Step 4: Make a scale for each axis (on Y-axis each large square box = 10 seats. On X-axis each large square box represents a political party).

Step 5: Make bars of equal width at equal distance on X-axis according to the given information: A = 80, B = 55, C = 36, D = 25, E = 10, F = 30.

Remember: The graphs used in example 2 and example 3 are known as simple bar graphs.

Practice-1: The following table shows the number of copies of a book a publishing house distributed to the dealers in each year from 2015 to 2022. Use bar graph to illustrate the above information. Years: 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022. No. of copies: 50,000, 40,000, 55,000, 30,000, 60,000, 70,000, 75,000, 90,000.

Multiple bar graphs — Example 4

“A graph that shows the conformation/data through multiple bars on the graph is called multiple bar graph.” Each data value is represented by a column in the same graph.

Example 4: Nadeem is a vegetable shop owner. He recorded the number of kilograms of vegetables sold over two days period. The results are listed on the table below. Create a multiple bar graph to display the data. At the end, list three conclusions that can be made about the data.

Vegetables1st day sale2nd day sale

Tomatoes50kg55kg

Steps of drawing a multiple (vertical) bar graph:

Step 1: Draw two lines XX′ and YY′ on the graph paper. Both lines are perpendicular to each other and cut at point ‘0’. The horizontal line is called X-axis and the vertical line is called Y-axis.

Step 2: Give title as “multiple bar graph for vegetables.”

Step 3: Label X-axis as “type of vegetables” and Y-axis as vegetables sold (kg).

Step 4: Make a key for bars of data (one colour for 1st day, another colour for 2nd day).

Step 5: Make bars of equal width and at equal distance on X-axis, two bars side by side for each vegetable, up to the 1st day and 2nd day values in the table.

Step 6: Three conclusions from the data: (a) Potato sold the most on both days (55kg, then 60kg). (b) Every vegetable except Peas sold more on the 2nd day than on the 1st day; Peas fell from 50kg to 40kg. (c) Cauliflower sold the least on the 1st day (30kg).

Reading a multiple bar graph — Example 5

Example 5: The graph in the book shows the number of students enrolled in two different schools of Lahore. Read the graph and answer: (i) Make a table for enrolled students of both schools. (ii) How many less students enrolled in school-B in year 2020 than 2019? (iii) How many total number of students enrolled in school-A in 5 years? (iv) How many total students enrolled in 2017 in both schools?

Step 1: (ii) 600 students − 300 students = 300 students.

Step 2: (iii) 400 + 700 + 600 + 800 + 200 = 2700. Hence, 2700 students enrolled in school-A in 5 years.

Step 3: (iv) 700 students + 400 students = 1100 students.

Final answer: (ii) 300 less students (iii) 2700 students (iv) 1100 students.

Practice-2: Draw a multiple bar graph for the below set of data that shows the obtained marks of two students. Ali: Maths 35, English 25, Urdu 28, Science 37, Islamiyat 45, GK 48. Ahmed: Maths 40, English 30, Urdu 45, Science 35, Islamiyat 25, GK 40.

lessons.title: 11.3.2 Pie Chart
lessons.notes_html:
Pie Chart

A graph in which data is represented by “pie chart” or sector of circle is known as pie graph. When we have many quantities in data, we use a pie graph or pie chart to represent these quantities. It shows the contribution of each value to the total.

The book's opening pie graph shows the working stages of population of Pakistan: Before working age (1–7) years 57% (205°), Working age (18–65) years 36% (130°), After working age (65+) years 7% (25°).

Reading a pie graph

We know that a circle has an angle of 360°. In a pie chart, the values/quantities are represented by sectors of a circle. It is useful to show or compare various quantities.

Example 6: Waqar did a survey in his school where he asked all the children to name their favourite colours. The results are shown in the pie chart. If there are 800 students in the school, then study the pie graph and answer the following questions: (i) Which is the most favourite colour among the students, and how many students like this colour? (ii) Which is the least favourite colour among students? Also, tell how many number of students like this colour? (iii) How many more students like blue colour than black colour? (iv) How many students like red colour? The pie chart shows: Orange 38%, Red 25%, Blue 19%, Black 18%.

Solution: Total number of students in the school = 800 students.

Step 1: (i) The most favourite colour among students is orange because its representing sector is the largest in the pie graph. Orange colour sector represents = 38%. Number of students like orange colour = 38% of 800 = 38/100 × 800 = 304 students.

Step 2: (ii) The least favourite colour among students is black because the representing sector is the smallest in the pie graph. Black colour represents = 18%. Number of students like black colour = 18% of 800 = 18/100 × 800 = 144 students.

Step 3: (iii) Blue sector represents = 19%. Number of students like blue colour = 19% of 800 = 19/100 × 800 = 152 students. Now, blue sector's students − black sector's students = 152 − 144 = 8 students. Therefore, 8 more students like blue colour than black colour.

Step 4: (iv) Red sector represents = 25%. Number of students like red sector = 25% of 800 = 25/100 × 800 = 200 students.

Final answer: (i) Orange, 304 students (ii) Black, 144 students (iii) 8 more students (iv) 200 students.

Drawing a pie chart

To draw a pie chart for given data, follow the following steps:

Step 1: (i) Draw a circle of any radius.

Step 2: (ii) Find the central angle of each sector by using the formula.

Angle of sector = (Value of the sector ÷ Total value) × 360°

Step 3: (iii) Join the centre to the circle. (iv) Start with the horizontal radius and draw radii making angles corresponding to the value of respective sectors. (v) Repeat the process for all the data values or groups. (vi) At the end shade every sector of the data values of different colours.

Example 7: Rabia wrote her daily time table on a paper and wanted to draw a pie chart of her time table. How can she draw the graph? If she spent her time as follow: Sleeping 8 hours, School 6 hours, Watching T.V 5 hours, Homework 3 hours, Playing 2 hours.

ActivitiesSleepingSchoolWatching T.VHomeworkPlaying
Time (hours)86532

Solution: Total number of hours in a day = 24.

Step 1: Angle of sleeping sector = (8 hours ÷ 24 hours) × 360° = 120°.

Step 2: Angle of school sector = (6 hours ÷ 24 hours) × 360° = 90°.

Step 3: Angle of T.V sector = (5 hours ÷ 24 hours) × 360° = 75°.

Step 4: Angle of homework sector = (3 hours ÷ 24 hours) × 360° = 45°.

Step 5: Angle of playing sector = (2 hours ÷ 24 hours) × 360° = 30°.

Step 6: Check: 120° + 90° + 75° + 45° + 30° = 360°. Now, construct the pie chart using the angle of each sector, starting from the horizontal radius, and shade each sector in a different colour with a key: Sleeping time, School time, T.V watching time, Playing time, Home work time.

Final answer: The pie chart has sectors of 120° (sleeping), 90° (school), 75° (watching T.V), 45° (homework) and 30° (playing).

Worked examples — Exercise 11.3

Q.1 Mr. Shahid gave his class surprise tests at the beginning and end of year. The given pie charts shows the grades. Study the pie graphs, do you think he must be happy with the results? (The two pie charts show the shares of A-grades, B-grades, C-grades, D-grades and F-grades at the beginning of the year and at the end of term; no percentage numbers are printed on these two charts.)

Step 1: Compare the two pie charts sector by sector using the key (A-grades, B-grades, C-grades, D-grades, F-grades).

Step 2: In the end of term result chart, the sectors for the better grades cover a larger part of the circle than in the beginning result chart, so the class performance has improved.

Final answer: He must be happy because the end of term result is better (as given in the book's Answers).

Q.2 The pie graph shows the percentage of obtained marks. If Waqas obtained 300 marks out of 400 marks, then study the graph and find the marks obtained in each subject. Also, tell in which subjects Waqas obtained maximum and minimum marks? The pie graph shows: English 25%, Science 20%, Mathematics 30%, Urdu 10%, Islamiyat 15% (percentages of the 300 marks obtained).

Step 1: English marks = 25% of 300 = 25/100 × 300 = 75.

Step 2: Science marks = 20% of 300 = 20/100 × 300 = 60.

Step 3: Mathematics marks = 30% of 300 = 30/100 × 300 = 90.

Step 4: Urdu marks = 10% of 300 = 10/100 × 300 = 30.

Step 5: Islamiyat marks = 15% of 300 = 15/100 × 300 = 45.

Step 6: Check: 75 + 60 + 90 + 30 + 45 = 300. The largest share is Mathematics (30%) and the smallest share is Urdu (10%).

Final answer: English 75, Science 60, Mathematics 90, Urdu 30, Islamiyat 45; maximum marks in Mathematics and minimum marks in Urdu.

Q.3 Aleezey is using social media network regularly. The following pie graph is showing the result of likes, comments, inbox massages and shares on her posts in the month of June 2022. Study the pie graph and answer the given questions. Aleezey received 6000 likes, comments and shares on her posts then. The pie graph shows: Likes 55%, Comments 35%, Inbox Messages 7%, Shares 3% (shares as recorded in the book's Answers). (i) Find the number of likes, comments, inbox messages and shares on Aleezey's posts. (ii) How many more likes are there than comments? (iii) How many less shares are there than likes? (iv) How many inbox messages are there?

Step 1: Likes = 55% of 6000 = 55/100 × 6000 = 3300.

Step 2: Comments = 35% of 6000 = 35/100 × 6000 = 2100.

Step 3: Inbox messages = 7% of 6000 = 7/100 × 6000 = 420.

Step 4: Shares = 3% of 6000 = 3/100 × 6000 = 180.

Step 5: (ii) More likes than comments = 3300 − 2100 = 1200.

Step 6: (iii) Less shares than likes = 3300 − 180 = 3120.

Step 7: (iv) Inbox messages = 420 (from Step 3).

Final answer: (i) Likes 3,300, comments 2100, inbox messages 420, shares 180 (ii) 1200 (iii) 3,120 (iv) 420.

Q.4 Draw the pie charts for the following data tables: (i) The following table shows the amount of money raised through fund raising by a group of students. Income source: Charity walk Rs. 3000, Donation from parents Rs. 2500, Donation from teachers Rs. 3200, Ticket selling Rs. 8400, Dressing-up-day Rs. 2500. (ii) The following table shows the number of students in a school who achieved each grade. Grades: Distinction 100, Merit 250, Pass 400, Fail 100.

Income sourceIncome (Rs.)
Charity walk3000
Donation from parents2500
Donation from teachers3200
Ticket selling8400
Dressing-up-day2500
GradesNumber of students
Distinction100
Merit250
Pass400
Fail100

Step 1: For (i), total income = 3000 + 2500 + 3200 + 8400 + 2500 = Rs. 19,600. Use the formula Angle of sector = (Value of the sector ÷ Total value) × 360° for each source.

Step 2: Charity walk angle = (3000 ÷ 19,600) × 360° = 55.1°. Donation from parents angle = (2500 ÷ 19,600) × 360° = 45.9°. Donation from teachers angle = (3200 ÷ 19,600) × 360° = 58.8°. Ticket selling angle = (8400 ÷ 19,600) × 360° = 154.3°. Dressing-up-day angle = (2500 ÷ 19,600) × 360° = 45.9°. Check: 55.1 + 45.9 + 58.8 + 154.3 + 45.9 = 360°.

Step 3: Draw a circle of any radius, start from the horizontal radius, draw radii at these angles one after another, shade each sector in a different colour and label it with a key.

Step 4: For (ii), total students = 100 + 250 + 400 + 100 = 850. Distinction angle = (100 ÷ 850) × 360° = 42.4°. Merit angle = (250 ÷ 850) × 360° = 105.9°. Pass angle = (400 ÷ 850) × 360° = 169.4°. Fail angle = (100 ÷ 850) × 360° = 42.4°. Check: 42.4 + 105.9 + 169.4 + 42.4 = 360.1° (difference is due to rounding).

Step 5: Draw a circle, mark the sectors with these angles from the horizontal radius, shade each sector differently and add the key: Distinction, Merit, Pass, Fail.

Final answer: (i) Sector angles about 55°, 46°, 59°, 154° and 46° (ticket selling is the largest sector). (ii) Sector angles about 42°, 106°, 169° and 42° (Pass is the largest sector).

mcqs.q: In a pie chart, the data values are represented by:
mcqs.why: A pie chart represents values by sectors of a circle; it shows the contribution of each value to the total, and a full circle has an angle of 360 degrees.

mcqs.q: The formula for the angle of a sector in a pie chart is:
options: Angle = (Total value / Value of sector) x 360 degrees
Angle = Value of sector x Total value x 360 degrees
Angle = (Value of the sector / Total value) x 360 degrees
Angle = (Value of the sector / Total value) x 100 degrees
mcqs.why: The lesson's formula is: Angle of sector = (Value of the sector / Total value) x 360 degrees, because the sectors must together fill the full 360 degrees of the circle.

mcqs.q: In the favourite colours survey of 800 students, orange has 38%. How many students like orange?
mcqs.why: Number liking orange = 38% of 800 = 38/100 x 800 = 38 x 8 = 304 students. Orange has the largest sector, so it is the most favourite colour.

mcqs.q: In the same survey of 800 students (Orange 38%, Red 25%, Blue 19%, Black 18%), how many more students like blue than black?
mcqs.why: Blue = 19% of 800 = 19/100 x 800 = 152 students. Black = 18% of 800 = 18/100 x 800 = 144 students. Difference = 152 - 144 = 8 more students like blue.

mcqs.q: In the same survey, how many students like red (25%)?
mcqs.why: Number liking red = 25% of 800 = 25/100 x 800 = 25 x 8 = 200 students, as worked out step by step in Example 6.

mcqs.q: Rabia spends 8 hours sleeping out of 24 hours in a day. The angle of the sleeping sector in her pie chart is:
mcqs.why: Angle of sleeping sector = (Value / Total) x 360 degrees = (8 / 24) x 360 degrees = (1/3) x 360 degrees = 120 degrees.

mcqs.q: Rabia spends 2 hours playing out of 24 hours. The angle of the playing sector is:
mcqs.why: Angle of playing sector = (2 / 24) x 360 degrees = 720 / 24 = 30 degrees. The full check is 120 + 90 + 75 + 45 + 30 = 360 degrees.

mcqs.q: Waqas obtained 300 marks. His pie graph gives Mathematics 30% of the obtained marks. His Mathematics marks are:
mcqs.why: Mathematics marks = 30% of 300 = 30/100 x 300 = 30 x 3 = 90 marks. This is the largest share, so Mathematics is his maximum subject.

mcqs.q: Aleezey received 6000 likes, comments, messages and shares in total, with Likes 55%. How many likes did she receive?
mcqs.why: Likes = 55% of 6000 = 55/100 x 6000 = 55 x 60 = 3300 likes, as calculated in the worked example for this pie graph.

mcqs.q: For the fund-raising data (total income Rs. 19,600), ticket selling raised Rs. 8,400. The angle of the ticket selling sector is about:
mcqs.why: Angle = (Value / Total) x 360 degrees = (8400 / 19600) x 360 degrees = 0.4286 x 360 degrees = 154.3 degrees, the largest sector in that pie chart.

lessons.title: 11.4 CALCULATION OF MEAN, MEDIAN AND MODE
lessons.notes_html:
Measures of central tendency

The most common numerical measures in statistical data are mean, median and mode. These measures are also called averages in statistics. These are also known as measures of central tendency.

“Central tendency of data is the value that represents the whole data or the stages at which the largest number of items tends to concentrate and so it is called central tendency.”

(a) Mean

In order to find the mean of few number of quantities, first we add then divide them by the total number of quantities. It can be calculated by formula.

Mean = Sum of quantities/values ÷ Number of quantities/values

The book's picture example: the masses of 5 children are 37kg, 45kg, 48kg, 45kg and 60kg. Sum = 37 + 45 + 48 + 45 + 60 = 235kg. Mean = 235 ÷ 5 = 47kg.

Example 8: The height of 5 children is 1.7 metre, 1.9 metre, 1.4 metre, 1.6 metre and 1.3 metre. Find the mean height of the children.

Step 1: Write the formula: Mean height = Sum of heights ÷ Number of children.

Step 2: Sum of heights = 1.7 + 1.9 + 1.4 + 1.6 + 1.3 = 7.9.

Step 3: Mean height = 7.9 ÷ 5 = 1.58 m.

Final answer: Therefore, the mean height of each children is 1.58 m.

Example 9: The mean of Rs. 75, Rs. 45, Rs. 60 and x is Rs. 67.5. Calculate the value of x.

Step 1: Write the formula: Mean value = Sum of values ÷ Number of values.

Step 2: Put the values: 67.5 = (75 + 45 + 60 + x) ÷ 4 = (180 + x) ÷ 4.

Step 3: Multiply both sides by 4: 67.5 × 4 = 180 + x, so 270 = 180 + x.

Step 4: x = 270 − 180 = 90.

Final answer: Therefore, the required value of x is Rs. 90.

Practice-4: 1. In Lahore the temperature of five days in winter was 18°C, 19°C, 20°C, 17°C and 37°C. Find the mean of temperature. Solution: Sum = 18 + 19 + 20 + 17 + 37 = 111. Mean = 111 ÷ 5 = 22.2°C. 2. The mean of five numbers is printed as 10 in the book, with numbers 79, 94, x, 105 and 200; as printed this has no solution because 79 + 94 + 105 + 200 = 478 is already more than 5 × 10 = 50, so this practice item appears to contain a misprint.

(b) Median

“The median in statistics is the middle most value in the given set of data.”

In order to find the median, we simply arrange the values/data in an ascending or descending order, then find the middle values. The middle term can be calculated by using the following formula:

Middle term = ((n + 1) ÷ 2)th term, where n is total number of observations

Remember: If the given set of data is even then find the mean of two middle values to get median.

Example 10: Find the median of the following set of data 45, 42, 53, 61, 44, 59 and 64.

Step 1: n = 7. Middle term = (n + 1) ÷ 2 = (7 + 1) ÷ 2 = 4, so the median is the fourth term in the set of data.

Step 2: Arrange the data in ascending order: 42, 44, 45, 53, 59, 61, 64.

Step 3: The 4th term is 53.

Final answer: Hence, the median is 53.

Example 11: Find the median of 92, 49, 87, 75, 101, 69, 105, 80, 115 and 108.

Step 1: n = 10. Middle term = ((10 + 1) ÷ 2)th term = 5.5th term.

Step 2: Arrange the given set of data in ascending order: 49, 69, 75, 80, 87, 92, 101, 105, 108, 115.

Step 3: The two middle values are 87 (5th) and 92 (6th). Median = Mean of two middle values = (87 + 92) ÷ 2 = 89.5.

Final answer: Hence, the median is 89.5.

Practice-5: Find the median of the following set of data: (i) 7.5, 4.6, 2.9, 3.8, 7.5, 8.4, 5.9 (ii) 9.4, 8.7, 8.5, 7.4, 6.9, 8.9, 7.8, 9.9. Solution: (i) Ascending order: 2.9, 3.8, 4.6, 5.9, 7.5, 7.5, 8.4; n = 7, middle term = 4th term = 5.9. (ii) Ascending order: 6.9, 7.4, 7.8, 8.5, 8.7, 8.9, 9.4, 9.9; n = 8, median = (8.5 + 8.7) ÷ 2 = 8.6.

(c) Mode

“The value that appears most frequently in the set of data is called mode.”

A set of given data may have one mode, more than one mode, or no mode. In order to find the mode in the given set of data, we simply observe the data and write the most appeared value.

Example 12: Find the mode of 4, 4, 7, 8, 9, 13, 4, 13, 6, 0, 13, 15 and 13.

Step 1: Arrange the data in ascending order: 0, 4, 4, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 13, 13, 13, 13, 15.

Step 2: Count each value: 4 appears 3 times and 13 appears 4 times; 13 appears the most.

Final answer: As, the most appeared value is 13. Therefore, mode = 13.

Practice-6: From the following sizes of kids trousers, find the model size of trousers. 28, 30, 25, 37, 29, 25, 33, 34, 25, 27 and 25. Solution: 25 appears 4 times, more than any other size, so the modal (model) size is 25.

Worked examples — Exercise 11.4

Q.1 Find the mean of the following data: (i) 8, 9, 7, 14, 15, 10 and 20 (ii) 14kg, 13kg, 10kg, 15kg and 25kg (iii) 13m, 14m, 37m, 24m, 20m, 16m and 19m (iv) 2.4, 8.4, 7.8, 4.6, 7.7 and 9.7 (v) 134km, 415km, 168km, 250km, 424km, 342km and 241km (vi) 42.6°C, 34°C, 37°C, 41°C, 38.6°C, 42.6°C, and 40.3°C.

Step 1: Use the formula in every part: Mean = Sum of values ÷ Number of values.

Step 2: (i) Sum = 8 + 9 + 7 + 14 + 15 + 10 + 20 = 83. Mean = 83 ÷ 7 = 11.86 (approximately).

Step 3: (ii) Sum = 14 + 13 + 10 + 15 + 25 = 77. Mean = 77 ÷ 5 = 15.4kg.

Step 4: (iii) Sum = 13 + 14 + 37 + 24 + 20 + 16 + 19 = 143. Mean = 143 ÷ 7 = 20.4m (approximately; the book's answer is 20.4 m).

Step 5: (iv) Sum = 2.4 + 8.4 + 7.8 + 4.6 + 7.7 + 9.7 = 40.6. Mean = 40.6 ÷ 6 = 6.8 (approximately; the book's answer is 6.8).

Step 6: (v) Sum = 134 + 415 + 168 + 250 + 424 + 342 + 241 = 1974. Mean = 1974 ÷ 7 = 282km.

Step 7: (vi) Sum = 42.6 + 34 + 37 + 41 + 38.6 + 42.6 + 40.3 = 276.1. Mean = 276.1 ÷ 7 = 39.4°C (approximately).

Final answer: (i) 11.86 (ii) 15.4kg (iii) 20.4m (iv) 6.8 (v) 282km (vi) 39.4°C.

Q.2 Nadeem read a storybook of 150 pages in 6 days. What is his per day reading of book pages?

Step 1: Per day reading is the mean: Mean = Sum of values ÷ Number of values = Total pages ÷ Number of days.

Step 2: Mean = 150 ÷ 6 = 25.

Final answer: His per day reading is 25 pages.

Q.3 The marks obtained by the students of grade 6 in the subject of Mathematics are given below. 85, 84, 80, 70, 71, 90, 55, 45, 78, 33, and 39. Find the mean of obtained marks.

Step 1: Write the formula: Mean = Sum of values ÷ Number of values.

Step 2: Sum of marks = 85 + 84 + 80 + 70 + 71 + 90 + 55 + 45 + 78 + 33 + 39 = 730.

Step 3: Number of values = 11. Mean = 730 ÷ 11 = 66.4 (approximately).

Final answer: The mean of obtained marks is 66.4 marks.

Q.4 The mean of 10 numbers is 29.01, seven number of them are 10, 15, 18, 34, 45, 26 and 32. The remaining three numbers are equal to k. What is the value of k?

Step 1: Use the formula: Mean = Sum of values ÷ Number of values, so Sum of values = Mean × Number of values = 29.01 × 10 = 290.1.

Step 2: Sum of the seven known numbers = 10 + 15 + 18 + 34 + 45 + 26 + 32 = 180.

Step 3: The remaining three numbers are each k, so 3k = 290.1 − 180 = 110.1.

Step 4: k = 110.1 ÷ 3 = 36.7.

Final answer: k = 36.7.

Q.5 Find the mode and median for each set of data given in Q.1.

Step 1: (i) 8, 9, 7, 14, 15, 10, 20 in ascending order: 7, 8, 9, 10, 14, 15, 20. n = 7, middle term = 4th term = 10, so median = 10. Every value appears once, so no mode.

Step 2: (ii) 14kg, 13kg, 10kg, 15kg, 25kg in ascending order: 10, 13, 14, 15, 25. Median = middle (3rd) value = 14kg. No value repeats, so no mode.

Step 3: (iii) 13m, 14m, 37m, 24m, 20m, 16m, 19m in ascending order: 13, 14, 16, 19, 20, 24, 37. Median = 4th value = 19m. No mode.

Step 4: (iv) 2.4, 8.4, 7.8, 4.6, 7.7, 9.7 in ascending order: 2.4, 4.6, 7.7, 7.8, 8.4, 9.7. n = 6, median = mean of 3rd and 4th values = (7.7 + 7.8) ÷ 2 = 7.75. No mode.

Step 5: (v) 134km, 415km, 168km, 250km, 424km, 342km, 241km in ascending order: 134, 168, 241, 250, 342, 415, 424. Median = 4th value = 250km. No mode.

Step 6: (vi) 42.6°C, 34°C, 37°C, 41°C, 38.6°C, 42.6°C, 40.3°C in ascending order: 34, 37, 38.6, 40.3, 41, 42.6, 42.6. Median = 4th value = 40.3°C. The value 42.6 appears twice, more than any other, so mode = 42.6°C.

Final answer: (i) Median 10, no mode (ii) Median 14, no mode (iii) Median 19, no mode (iv) Median 7.75, no mode (v) Median 250, no mode (vi) Median 40.3, mode 42.6.

Q.6 The scores of 12 students in a Mathematics class test are 18, 17, 18, 13, 9, 11, 13, 24, 22, 18, 11, 18. Find the model score of the class.

Step 1: Count how often each score appears: 18 appears 4 times, 13 appears 2 times, 11 appears 2 times, and 17, 9, 24, 22 appear once each.

Step 2: The most frequently appeared value is the mode.

Final answer: The modal (model) score of the class is 18.

Q.7 Find the median of the given set of data 47.5, 40, 25.5, 27.7, 49.8, 32.4, 9.6, 8.4, 40. (One further value in this printed list is hidden under the book's watermark; the book's Answers give the median as 30.05.)

Step 1: Arrange the data in ascending order; the readable values in order are: 8.4, 9.6, 25.5, 27.7, 32.4, 40, 40, 47.5, 49.8.

Step 2: With the full printed set, the two middle values are 27.7 and 32.4.

Step 3: Median = Mean of two middle values = (27.7 + 32.4) ÷ 2 = 60.1 ÷ 2 = 30.05.

Final answer: The median is 30.05 (as given in the book's Answers).

mcqs.q: The mean of a set of quantities is calculated by:
options: Sum of values x Number of values
Sum of values / Number of values
The middle value after arranging the data
mcqs.why: The lesson's formula is Mean = Sum of quantities/values / Number of quantities/values: first add all the values, then divide by how many values there are.

mcqs.q: The masses of 5 children are 37 kg, 45 kg, 48 kg, 45 kg and 60 kg. Their mean mass is:
mcqs.why: Sum = 37 + 45 + 48 + 45 + 60 = 235 kg. Mean = Sum / Number of values = 235 / 5 = 47 kg.

mcqs.q: The heights of 5 children are 1.7 m, 1.9 m, 1.4 m, 1.6 m and 1.3 m. The mean height is:
The mean of Rs. 75, Rs. 45, Rs. 60 and x is Rs. 67.5. The value of x is:
mcqs.why: Sum = Mean x Number of values = 67.5 x 4 = 270. Known sum = 75 + 45 + 60 = 180. So x = 270 - 180 = 90, that is Rs. 90.

mcqs.q: Nadeem read a storybook of 150 pages in 6 days. His mean reading per day is:
mcqs.why: Mean per day = Total pages / Number of days = 150 / 6 = 25 pages per day.

mcqs.q: The median of a set of data is:
options: The value that appears most frequently
The sum of all values divided by their number
The middle most value in the given set of data
The difference between the largest and smallest values
mcqs.why: The median is the middle most value: arrange the data in ascending or descending order and take the middle value. The most frequent value is the mode instead.

mcqs.q: Find the median of 45, 42, 53, 61, 44, 59, 64.
mcqs.why: Arrange in ascending order: 42, 44, 45, 53, 59, 61, 64. Here n = 7, middle term = (7 + 1) / 2 = 4th term = 53, so the median is 53.
Ascending order: 49, 69, 75, 80, 87, 92, 101, 105, 108, 115. With n = 10 the two middle values are the 5th (87) and 6th (92). Median = (87 + 92) / 2 = 179 / 2 = 89.5.

mcqs.q: The mode of a set of data is:
options: The middle value of the arranged data
The mean of the two middle values
The sum of all the values
The value that appears most frequently in the set of data
mcqs.why: By definition, the mode is the value that appears most frequently in the set of data; a set may have one mode, more than one mode, or no mode.
Counting appearances: 4 appears 3 times and 13 appears 4 times, while every other value appears once. The most frequent value is 13, so the mode is 13.

chapters.title: Unit 12: Statistics and Probability — Sub-Domain 2: Probability

lessons.title: 12.1 EXPERIMENT
lessons.notes_html:
Introduction — Probability

Have you ever heard about a toss before the start of cricket match between two cricket teams (e.g. Pakistan and Indian cricket teams) on television (TV)? A coin is used for toss to decide that which team will bat first.

Similarly, there are many aspects of uncertainty and chances in our routine life. e.g. Will Pakistan cricket team win the match? If throw a dice will I score double of 5? It is likely to rain. Should I go outside with umbrella?

To overcome these types of situations we use the term “probability” in Mathematics. “Probability is the branch of Mathematics that measures how likely something will happen.”

We use it to find the probability of an outcome of an event. Here, we are going to learn a few basic concepts, probability formulas involved to calculate the probability of different types of situations.

Students' Learning Outcomes for this sub-domain: Explain experiments, outcomes, sample space, events, equally likely events and probability of a single event; Differentiate the outcomes that are equally likely and not equally likely to occur (including real-world word problems).

Experiment

In statistics “an experiment is any procedure that can be repeated many times and has a well defined sets of possible outcomes”. There are two kinds of experiments.

Scientific experiment

This is an experiment for which outcome can be predicted with certainty beforehand such as oxygen and hydrogen or add two numbers such as 4 and 5, etc.

Random experiment

An experiment for which the outcome cannot be predicted except that it is known to be one of the set of possible outcomes, is called a random experiment. e.g. for any given triangle, without knowing the three angles, we can clearly say that the sum of measures of interior angles of a triangle is 180°. Similarly, tossing a coin and rolling a dice, are examples of random experiment.

The book's table of experiments and possible outcomes: tossing a coin — possible outcomes Head and Tail; playing a dice game — possible outcomes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 shown by the dots on the dice; there are 4 green balls and 5 red balls in the bag, a ball is drawn at random — possible outcomes a green ball or a red ball.

Since, our interest lies in the random experiment, so in this text by experiment we mean random experiment.

mcqs.q: What is probability in Mathematics?
options: The branch of Mathematics that measures how likely something will happen
The branch of Mathematics that measures how long something is
The branch of Mathematics that measures how heavy something is
The branch of Mathematics that measures how fast something moves
mcqs.why: The notes define probability as the branch of Mathematics that measures how likely something will happen, used for uncertain situations.

mcqs.q: In a cricket match, a coin is used for the toss to decide what?
options: Which team has won the match
How many runs will be scored
mcqs.why: The notes give the cricket toss as an example: a coin is tossed before the match to decide which team will bat first.

mcqs.q: In statistics, what is an experiment?
options: A procedure that can be done only once in a laboratory
A game played between two teams
Any procedure that can be repeated many times and has a well defined set of possible outcomes
A question asked to a group of students
mcqs.why: The notes define an experiment as any procedure that can be repeated many times and has a well defined set of possible outcomes.

mcqs.q: A scientific experiment is an experiment for which the outcome:
options: Can never be known in any way
Is always decided by tossing a coin
Is always shown by the dots on a dice
Can be predicted with certainty beforehand
mcqs.why: For a scientific experiment, such as adding 4 and 5, the outcome can be predicted with certainty beforehand, unlike a random experiment.

mcqs.q: What is a random experiment?
options: An experiment whose outcome cannot be predicted, except that it is known to be one of the set of possible outcomes
An experiment whose outcome is known exactly before it is done
An experiment that is done only with chemicals
An experiment that has no possible outcomes at all
mcqs.why: In a random experiment the exact outcome cannot be predicted, but it is known to be one of the set of possible outcomes.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of a random experiment given in the notes?
mcqs.why: Tossing a coin and rolling a dice are given in the notes as examples of random experiments, because their outcomes cannot be predicted.

mcqs.q: What are the possible outcomes of tossing a coin?
mcqs.why: The book's table lists tossing a coin with possible outcomes Head and Tail, so either one may appear on a toss.

mcqs.q: In a dice game, what are the possible outcomes shown by the dots on the dice?
options: A green ball and a red ball
mcqs.why: The book's table lists playing a dice game with possible outcomes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, shown by the dots on the dice.

mcqs.q: There are 4 green balls and 5 red balls in a bag. A ball is drawn at random. What are the possible outcomes?
options: A green ball or a red ball
mcqs.why: The bag contains only green and red balls, so the book's table gives the possible outcomes as a green ball or a red ball.

mcqs.q: In this text, by the word 'experiment' we mean:
mcqs.why: The notes state that our interest lies in the random experiment, so in this text by experiment we mean random experiment.

lessons.title: 12.2 SAMPLE SPACE AND AN EVENT
lessons.notes_html:
Sample space

For a random experiment, the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment is called a sample space and is denoted by S. The elements of S are called sample points of outcomes.

Note: An element of the sample space is called sample point.

Remember — Outcome: A possible result of a random experiment is called its outcome.

For example:

Step 1: (i) Tossing a coin once, then S = {H, T}, where H and T are the possible outcomes (Head and Tail).

Step 2: (ii) Tossing a coin twice, then the possible outcomes in the sample space are {HH, HT, TH, TT}.

Step 3: (iii) Consider an experiment of rolling a dice. The possible outcomes of this experiment are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, if we are interested in the number of dots on the upper face on the dice.

Step 4: (iv) Rolling two dice, then we have sample space S = {(1,1) (1,2) (1,3) (1,4) (1,5) (1,6); (2,1) (2,2) (2,3) (2,4) (2,5) (2,6); (3,1) (3,2) (3,3) (3,4) (3,5) (3,6); (4,1) (4,2) (4,3) (4,4) (4,5) (4,6); (5,1) (5,2) (5,3) (5,4) (5,5) (5,6); (6,1) (6,2) (6,3) (6,4) (6,5) (6,6)} — 36 sample points in total.

Practice-1: Write down the sample space for tossing a coin three times. Solution: Each toss gives H or T, so S = {HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT} — 8 sample points.

Events

Let S be the sample space of an experiment. Any subset E of S is called an event associated with the experiment. For example E = {HH, TT} is an event associated with the experiment of tossing a coin twice. There are two types of events (with equally likely and not equally likely events also described in the book).

(i) Simple event

“An event which contains a single point of sample space is known as a simple event” e.g. S = {H, T} then E = {H} is a simple event.

(ii) Compound event

“An event which contains more than one point of sample space is called compound event.” e.g. If S = {HH, HT, TH, TT} then E1 = {HH, TT} and E2 = {HT, TH} represent compound events.

(iii) Equally Likely Events

Two events are said to be equally likely if they have equal chances of happening. For example when we toss a coin there are equal chances of getting a head or a tail. So, getting a head and tail by tossing a coin are equally likely events. When a dice is rolled then getting an odd number and getting an even number are equally likely events.

Note: Equally likely event is also known as fair event, and not equally likely event is also known as unfair event.

(iv) Not Equally Likely Events

An event is said to be not equally likely if one or more events are more likely to occur than others.

For example, if you were using a dice that always landed with six facing up, that would be not equally likely event. Similarly, a matchbox has 6 faces but all the faces are not equally likely. So, each face has different occuring value.

Project-1: Differentiate equally likely and not equally likely outcomes/events with examples from your surrounding.

lessons.title: 12.3 PROBABILITY OF SINGLE EVENT
lessons.notes_html:
Probability of a single event

We use a formula to calculate the probability of an event to occur. “How likely something is to occur / happen is called probability.”

Let S be the sample space of a random experiment, and E be an event. The probability that an event E will occur, is denoted by P(E). So,

Probability of an event occur = Number of favourable outcomes ÷ Total number of outcomes

P(E) = n(E) ÷ n(S)

Practice-2: Shahbaz and Amina has 4 new vehicles this year, 2 cars and 2 wagons. What is the probability that their next number will be a car? Solution: Total vehicles = 4, cars = 2, so P(car) = 2 ÷ 4 = 1/2.

Example 1: Find the Probability of getting an even number when a dice is rolled.

Step 1: Sample space S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, so n(S) = 6.

Step 2: The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6, so n(E) = 3.

Step 3: Use the formula: P(E) = n(E) ÷ n(S) = 3 ÷ 6 = 1/2.

Final answer: The probability of getting an even number is 1/2.

Example 2: (i) Find a probability that a tail will turn up if a coin is tossed. (ii) Find a probability that an odd number has shown up if a fair dice is tossed.

Step 1: (i) Here S = {H, T}. Let A = set of tails = {T}, n(A) = 1. Since the outcomes are equally likely, by using the formula P(A) = n(A) ÷ n(S) = 1/2.

Step 2: (ii) Here S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. Let B = set of odd numbers has shown up = {1, 3, 5}, n(B) = 3. Since the outcomes are equally likely then we have P(B) = n(B) ÷ n(S) = 3/6 = 1/2.

Final answer: (i) 1/2 (ii) 1/2.

Remember: The probability of an event is always a number from 0 to 1 (inclusive), shown on the probability scale: 0 = Impossible, then Unlikely, Even chance or equally likely in the middle, then Likely, and 1 = Certain.

Do you Know? If the probability of an event occurring is ‘0’, we call it an impossible event. If the probability of an event occurring is ‘1’, we call it certain event.

Example 3: Aleezey is playing cards with her friend when she draws a card from a pack of 56 cards numbered from 1 to 56. What is probability of drawing a number that is perfect of square?

Step 1: Here S = {1, 2, 3, …, 56}, so n(S) = 56.

Step 2: B = Set of perfect square numbers = {1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49}, so n(B) = 7.

Step 3: Since the outcomes are equally likely then we have P(B) = n(B) ÷ n(S) = 7/56 = 1/8.

Final answer: The probability of drawing a perfect square number is 1/8.

Worked examples — Exercise 12.1

Q.1 Each of the letters in the words Jammu Kashmir are on separate cards, face down on the table. If you pick a card at random, what is the probability that its letters will be J and K?

Step 1: Write the letters of “Jammu Kashmir” (without the space): J, A, M, M, U, K, A, S, H, M, I, R. Total number of cards n(S) = 12.

Step 2: The letter J appears once and the letter K appears once, so the favourable outcomes (the card is J or K) = 1 + 1 = 2.

Step 3: Use the formula: P(E) = n(E) ÷ n(S) = 2/12 = 1/6. Separately, P(J) = 1/12 and P(K) = 1/12.

Final answer: The probability that the card shows J or K is 1/6 (the probability for J alone is 1/12 and for K alone is 1/12).

Q.2 What is the probability of rolling a dice at: (i) rolling a ‘5’? (ii) rolling a number greater than ‘6’? (iii) rolling a number less than or equal to ‘3’?

Step 1: For one dice, S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, n(S) = 6.

Step 2: (i) Only one outcome is 5, so n(E) = 1 and P(E) = n(E) ÷ n(S) = 1/6.

Step 3: (ii) No outcome on a dice is greater than 6, so n(E) = 0 and P(E) = 0/6 = 0 (an impossible event).

Step 4: (iii) The numbers less than or equal to 3 are 1, 2 and 3, so n(E) = 3 and P(E) = 3/6 = 1/2.

Final answer: (i) 1/6 (ii) 0 (iii) 1/2.

Q.3 Two unbiased coins are tossed what is the probability of obtaining: (i) all tails (ii) one head (iii) one tail (iv) all heads.

Step 1: The sample space is S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}, so n(S) = 4.

Step 2: (i) All tails = {TT}, n(E) = 1, so P(E) = n(E) ÷ n(S) = 1/4.

Step 3: (ii) One head = {HT, TH}, n(E) = 2, so P(E) = 2/4 = 1/2.

Step 4: (iii) One tail = {HT, TH}, n(E) = 2, so P(E) = 2/4 = 1/2.

Step 5: (iv) All heads = {HH}, n(E) = 1, so P(E) = 1/4.

Final answer: (i) 1/4 (ii) 1/2 (iii) 1/2 (iv) 1/4.

Q.4 There are 5 green colours, 3 red colours and 4 blue colours in a box. What is the probability that: (i) all colours are green (ii) all colours are blue. (Solved for one colour drawn at random from the box.)

Step 1: Total number of colours n(S) = 5 + 3 + 4 = 12.

Step 2: (i) Green colours = 5, so P(green) = n(E) ÷ n(S) = 5/12.

Step 3: (ii) Blue colours = 4, so P(blue) = 4/12 = 1/3.

Final answer: (i) 5/12 (ii) 1/3.

Q.5 Consider a random experiment of tossing three coins each coin toss only once. (i) Find the sample space S if we want to determine the exact sequence of tails and heads obtained. (ii) Find the probability of two tails only.

Step 1: (i) Each coin gives H or T, so S = {HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT} and n(S) = 8.

Step 2: (ii) The outcomes with exactly two tails are HTT, THT and TTH, so n(E) = 3.

Step 3: Use the formula: P(E) = n(E) ÷ n(S) = 3/8.

Final answer: (i) S = {HHH, HHT, HTH, THH, HTT, THT, TTH, TTT} (ii) 3/8.

Q.6 What is the probability of number at least 5 when two dice are rolling once. Also find the probability of number at least 1. (Solved as in the book's Answers: the probability that the number 5 shows on at least one of the two dice, and that the number 1 shows on at least one of the two dice.)

Step 1: For two dice, n(S) = 36 (the 36 pairs listed in section 12.2).

Step 2: The pairs in which 5 shows at least once are (1,5), (2,5), (3,5), (4,5), (5,5), (6,5), (5,1), (5,2), (5,3), (5,4), (5,6) — 11 pairs, so n(E) = 11.

Step 3: P(E) = n(E) ÷ n(S) = 11/36.

Step 4: In the same way, the pairs in which 1 shows at least once are also 11, so the probability = 11/36.

Final answer: 11/36 and 11/36.

Q.7 There are 200 Covid-19 patients in a private hospital in Lahore. Of these 20 are selected to undergo a special treatment that increases the percentage cured rate from 60% to 85%. What is the probability that a patient received a special treatment if the patient is known to be cured?

Step 1: Patients with special treatment = 20, cured at 85%: 85% of 20 = 17 patients cured.

Step 2: Patients without special treatment = 200 − 20 = 180, cured at 60%: 60% of 180 = 108 patients cured.

Step 3: Total cured patients = 17 + 108 = 125.

Step 4: Use the formula: P(E) = n(E) ÷ n(S) = cured patients who received special treatment ÷ all cured patients = 17/125 = 0.136.

Final answer: The probability is 17/125 (0.136).

Q.8 Two girl students and two boy students enter in a classroom and take 4 seats random in a row. What is the probability that the boy students take the two end seats?

Step 1: Total ways for 4 different students to take 4 seats in a row = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24, so n(S) = 24.

Step 2: Favourable ways: the 2 boys take the two end seats in 2 × 1 = 2 ways, and the 2 girls take the two middle seats in 2 × 1 = 2 ways, so n(E) = 2 × 2 = 4.

Step 3: Use the formula: P(E) = n(E) ÷ n(S) = 4/24 = 1/6.

Final answer: The probability that the boy students take the two end seats is 1/6.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the probability of an event E?
mcqs.why: The notes give P(E) = n(E) / n(S), that is, number of favourable outcomes divided by total number of outcomes.

mcqs.q: Shahbaz and Amina have 4 new vehicles: 2 cars and 2 wagons. What is the probability that their next vehicle will be a car?
mcqs.why: Favourable outcomes = cars = 2, total outcomes = vehicles = 4, so P(car) = 2 / 4 = 1/2, as worked in Practice-2.

mcqs.q: What is the probability of getting an even number when a dice is rolled?
mcqs.why: Even numbers are 2, 4 and 6, so favourable outcomes = 3 and total outcomes = 6, giving P(E) = 3 / 6 = 1/2.

mcqs.q: The probability of an event is always a number:
mcqs.why: The notes show probability on a scale from 0 to 1: 0 means impossible, 1 means certain, and even chance lies in the middle.

mcqs.q: Aleezey draws a card from a pack of 56 cards numbered 1 to 56. What is the probability of drawing a perfect square number?
mcqs.why: Perfect squares up to 56 are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, so favourable outcomes = 7 and total outcomes = 56, giving P = 7 / 56 = 1/8.

mcqs.q: The letters of 'Jammu Kashmir' are on 12 separate cards. What is the probability that a card picked at random shows J or K?
mcqs.why: J appears once and K appears once, so favourable outcomes = 1 + 1 = 2 and total outcomes = 12, giving P = 2 / 12 = 1/6.

mcqs.q: What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 6 on a dice?
mcqs.why: No dice outcome is greater than 6, so favourable outcomes = 0 and total outcomes = 6, giving P = 0 / 6 = 0, an impossible event.

mcqs.q: Two unbiased coins are tossed. What is the probability of obtaining all tails?
mcqs.why: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}, so total outcomes = 4. All tails is {TT}, favourable outcomes = 1, giving P = 1 / 4.

mcqs.q: There are 5 green, 3 red and 4 blue colours in a box. One colour is drawn at random. What is the probability it is blue?
mcqs.why: Blue colours = 4 and total colours = 5 + 3 + 4 = 12, so favourable / total = 4 / 12 = 1/3.

mcqs.q: Three coins are tossed once each. What is the probability of getting exactly two tails?
mcqs.why: Total outcomes = 8. Exactly two tails are HTT, THT and TTH, so favourable outcomes = 3, giving P = 3 / 8.
